en: The Essence of Awakening.
Oṃ! Out of mere curiosity and with the desire to please the wise, [I shall compose this].
Having performed the auspicious invocation, the Essence of Enlightenment (Bodhasāra) is now set forth.
We worship Gaṇeśa, the sovereign of the hosts, the power of the Supreme Self who is filled with a multitude of infinite powers, and who destroys all obstacles.
I remember with devotion that Sarasvatī, the power of knowledge, who abides in her own nature through both luminosity and reflective awareness.
I pay homage to the venerable gurus, whose very nature is supreme bliss;
their compassion dispels the threefold suffering and is a fountain of the nectar of Brahman.
Now, the praise of the Guru:
Homage to the illustrious Guru-Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the cruel Madhu and Kaiṭabha known as Mada and Moha, and the abode of the goddess of liberation.
The triad of Hari, Brahmā, and Hara have attained greatness through their qualities;
our gurus, however, have attained true guru-hood by having transcended all qualities.
Rudra is the destroyer of the end of the city; Hari is the slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin;
Caṇḍī is the remover of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; and the Guru is the remover of all dualities.
When satisfied, the deities bestow wealth, longevity, sons, and fame;
but who indeed will grant knowledge without the sandals of the venerable Guru?
Victorious indeed is the quality of the pollen from the lotus-feet of the venerable Guru,
by which alone the three qualities— rajas, sattva, and tamas— are destroyed.
We are those who must cross; awakening is the boat, and the ocean of existence is what is to be crossed.
Therefore, I worship the glorious Guru, the savior, who acts as the helmsman for that crossing.
Having become a guru through the instruction of Tāraka, he is the bestower of liberation;
therefore, the Lord (Īśvara) in Kāśī is a guru even greater than that Īśvara.
Through the grace of the Guru one attains the Lord; through the grace of the Lord, one attains the Guru.
However, the vision of the venerable Guru is the cause for the supreme vision of the Lord.
Because He is the cause of everything, the Lord is the cause of both saṃsāra and liberation;
He is the teacher of liberation alone. Therefore, there is no reality higher than the Teacher.
Indeed, liberation may occur anywhere through the greatness of the Guru even without the greatness of the sacred field; but it does not occur at Kāśī without a Guru.
"What should be said as 'May you forgive me,' or what should be uttered as 'Be gracious'? My Guru is by his very nature already filled with forgiveness and grace. (NBs 1.15)
Now, the discernment of the disciple:
the seed is indeed the instruction of the guru, and the seeker of knowledge is called the field.
The tree of awakening grows from the sprout of discernment, and liberation is its fruit.
Although a tree does not arise without both the field and the seed,
nevertheless, the seed is called the substantial cause (upādāna) and the field is called the efficient condition (nimitta).
The tree is the transformation of the seed, not the transformation of the field;
awakening is the transformation of the teacher, not the transformation of the disciple.
For a tree belongs to the class of seeds, not to the class of fields;
for awakening belongs to the class of teachers, not to the class of disciples. (NBs 2.4)

Just as a tree of the same species as the seed is produced when it is sown in the field, so too is an awakening of the same nature as the teacher’s own self imparted to the disciple by the teacher. (NBs 2.5)

For the light of a fire, residing in the wick, dispels darkness and shines; it is the light itself, which is the destroyer of darkness and whose nature is illumination, that does so, and not the wick.
For it is the light of the Guru residing in the disciple that destroys darkness and shines forth;
the one who destroys darkness and whose nature is light is the Guru alone, not the disciple.
When fire, having ascended a piece of wood, reduces a city to ashes, the cause of that reduction to ashes is the quality of fire itself; it does not reside in the wood.
The Guru, having entered the disciple by means of the nature of awakening, burns away duality in an instant;
it is the settled conclusion that this is the power of the Guru, not of the disciple.
Just as a lotus blossoms when the sun rises,
so too do lotuses made of wood, stone, or clay fail to shine.
Just as the sun, being a source of light, causes only the lotus to blossom, so too the teacher, being an awakener, awakens only the disciple. (NBs 2.11)
The greatness of the illuminator is indeed greater than that of the illuminated;
listen now as I shall describe that subtle distinction of the Guru-sun. (NBs 2.12)
Ah! By means of the Vedāntic reasonings joined with specific discrimination and dispassion, the sun-like Guru leads the disciple—who, though distinct from him—to oneness with himself. (NBs 2.13)
Even the sun, though it causes expansion, cannot bring the lotus to its own state of identity;
therefore, the sandals of the venerable Guru should be served with one's entire being.
That is true: without both the donor and the recipient, giving is not accomplished.
Nevertheless, while the recipient may be a worthy vessel, the donor is the primary cause.
Through contact with a touchstone, iron may become gold, yet it is not that stone;
but through contact with the touchstone of the Guru, that very [iron] becomes [gold] in an instant.
Thus, O wise one, the utility of both [the teacher and the sandals] is equal when distinguished;
the disciple would be merely the instrumental cause, while the Guru’s sandals are the most venerable.
"O Rāma, the sequence of instruction is merely for the sake of maintaining order"—such statements as these are intended to increase the enthusiasm of the disciple. (NBs 2.18)
This definitive conclusion of all systems, which produces immediate conviction, should always be cultivated as the determination regarding the teacher and the disciple. (NBs 2.19)
The desire to know Brahman;
now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman; Brahman alone is that which is to be known.
Now, [the definition is established] through both an incidental definition and a definition of the essential nature.
In such [scriptural] passages as "The Lord is the fundamental cause of origination, subsistence, and destruction;
he is omniscient and his volition is true," [the Lord is described as] being extrinsic (taṭastha).
That which is of the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss, self-luminous, and higher than the highest—
described in the Vedas as "not atomic" and so forth— is indeed the definition of its own essential nature.
Whatever is required, whether as a subordinate or a primary factor,
all that is explained here under the guise of various chapters.
Regarding the sequence of external and internal means of accomplishment:
whatever is internal is explained after that which is external.
The Foundation for Detachment:
O one of noble mind, first hear the foundation for detachment.
If even the rim does not exist there, what kind of stability can the wheel have?
The Vedic consecration does not exist in a Śūdra, nor does oil [exist] in sand;
there are no hairs on the palm of the hand, and likewise, there is no liberation for one who possesses passion.
Dispassion is of two kinds, subtle; understand its distinction:
one is primarily characterized by the desire to know, and the other is primarily characterized by the desire to abandon.
O Sage, both the desire to abandon transmigratory existence and the inquiry into Brahman are one and the same;
nevertheless, there is indeed a certain distinction between them here.
Those who have fallen from their kingdom, those afflicted by chronic illness, those dependent on others, and those whose prosperity has been destroyed—
when they practice asceticism out of detachment, that is primarily the desire to abandon [the world].
For those steadfast ones who, free from mental anguish, physical disease, fear, agitation, dependence on others, and so forth, desire liberation— listen to this method for them.

Those in whose homes dwell the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and whose residence is in the Nandana grove— Kaśyapa and the others who perform austerities— this is indeed primarily for the sake of testing [the Lord].
Those living beings who, afflicted by mental anguish, physical disease, fear, agitation, dependence on others, and so forth, desire liberation— that indeed is the primary state of renunciation.
Human birth has been attained, which is difficult to find, and the intellect has been refined by the true scriptures;
yet if there is no rest in Brahman, then what have we truly achieved?
Thus, by means of such resolve—like one who falls for the fruit in the sky—the wise investigate; that indeed is the preeminence of inquiry.
Virocana, Kārtavīrya, Bali, Śrī Rāghava, and others—
these are indeed the examples therein, for they were dispassionate toward royal pleasures.

If the inquiry into Brahman arises from an intense detachment from saṃsāra, that detachment consists primarily in the desire to abandon [the cycle of existence] on the part of those whose lives are rooted in merit. (NBs 4.1.12)
O dear one, that dispassion toward all objects of perception which is brought about by an intense desire to know Brahman is indeed the primary goal of such inquiry.
For one whose dispassion is innate, what need is there to speak of its preeminence?
Now, the defects [of the world] are demonstrated, for dispassion arises from the perception of these defects.
I shall speak in brief; listen with an attentive mind, O virtuous one, concerning the inconsistency [of the self] starting from the body.
This mockery of the body, which they adorn with gold, garments, and even sandalwood paste.
It is precisely through a lack of investigation that this body has come to be regarded as delightful.
By what means could there be any loveliness in this body, which is edible by carnivores, which is but fuel for the fire, and which is emaciated by its own transformation?
This place is the abode of Kali; this is a physical conflict, and this is the dwelling of the five elements. How could one be happy there?
The womb is a prison; childhood is nothing but sheer delusion.
Even there, existence is utterly unbearable due to total dependence on others.
Wherein there is the pain of the arrows of desire, the fever of separation from a beloved woman,
an abundance of accumulated sins, and youth that is a forest of calamities.
The body of an old man, having become uneven with protrusions and depressions and greyed by the corrosion of age, is as loathsome as a rotten pumpkin gourd.
What more need be said of death? From that comes the fear of the messengers of Death;
in hell there is great suffering, and in heaven there is the fear born of falling.
Even there, there is the mockery of being high or low;
if one were to be born in the womb of an animal or similar state, what need is there to speak of suffering?
Rebirth, repeated death, repeated suffering, and repeated fear— the living being,
submerged in the ocean of delusion, does not know its destination.
In the duty of a Kṣatriya, there is the mockery of conduct; for there is supreme violence in it, and great meanness in begging.
In commerce, untruth is indeed not a sin greater than falsehood itself.
In service there is supreme hardship; as a farmer, one is like a worm in the soil.
In gambling there may be the loss of all one's possessions; in theft there is great fear of the king.
No substance falls from the sky; how then could a livelihood that provides pleasure not be a mockery of desire?
When life has departed, the piśācas devour great flesh;
while still alive, men and women with four faces devour each other’s flesh.
At night, piśācas dance in cremation grounds with human bodies,
while householders dance in their homes with various arrangements of limbs.
The deluded one repeatedly licks, touches, smells, and eats;
this establishment of vulgar practices is consistent with the nature of a village lion.
Is that pleasure which arises from scratching an itch truly pleasure? It is not; for just as there is great pain afterwards, so too is sensual pleasure.
A hunter cuts down the deer attached to sound with sharp arrows;
a woman repeatedly cuts a man attached to form with the knife of passion.
Mocked by his own wrath, he drinks his own blood and dances in the darkness by day.
A cruel and wrathful person terrifies himself by means of his own self; he is not a true Rākṣasa.
The mockery of greed is neither piśācas, nor ḍākinīs, nor serpents, nor scorpions.
Just as greed, that enemy of the intellect, causes a person to become bewildered.
Meru, resembling a drop of clarified butter in the forest fire of insatiable desire, how then could even thousands or lakhs of such things ever satisfy one possessed by greed?
Wandering through dreams even while awake from morning until sleepless night, one finds no peace; this is the prowess of greed.
When yakṣas, serpents, and the like diligently guard a treasure, they neither drink nor eat; for their gurus are indeed deceitful.
And as for the wealth of the wealthy, which is devoid of both giving and enjoyment,
not even a speck of dust is given from it to those who guard the earth.
Does a fool place his wealth in a vessel made of copper?
While the wealth held in the vessel is auspicious, O noble one, examine the vessel itself.
For the sake of wealth that is like crow-dung, the wealthy—who are blinded by intoxication—are served with great physical hardship; this is a profound mockery.
Jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like do not serve to increase greed;
even one who praises jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is himself devoted to greed.
Meditating on some tiny fragment of wealth, you gaze upon the face of the rich man;
like a dog, you offer flatteries—remember that which was done out of greed.
It is an iron bolt, a destroyer of prosperity, marked by restlessness, and a source of fear;
because it cuts through both worlds, it is proclaimed as "greed" (lobha).
Those with desires are greedy for women; those without desires are greedy for liberation.
For the Blessed One is greedy for existence, while one who is entirely free from greed is extremely rare to find.
On a bed bright with the foam of milk, attended at her feet by a young maiden,
the king finds no sleep due to his desire to conquer the kingdoms of others.
Thieves encountered on the road and friendship grew between them;
they departed taking the wealth, while the dull-witted one grieved behind them.
But the master protects his wealth from here and there like a thief,
while the wife, sons, and others enjoy the master's property as if they were thieves.
That wealth which people conceal from their sons, friends, and wives—I consider that to be a sin; for merit is never concealed.
That passionate courtesan is indeed excellent who desires wealth; fie upon that talkative man, greedy for riches, who speaks of dispassion!
The reciter of scriptures boasts after taking wealth from the wealthy,
just as a courtesan does after uniting with many wealthy men.
In the same way, this greedy person who recites the Vedānta does not shine,
just like one wearing matted hair and smeared with ashes who has been placed in shackles for theft.
If the learned attain prestige solely through the acquisition of wealth,
then describe what distinction there is between a courtesan and a scholar!
O Maheśvara, do not show your face to this man who speaks of things as impermanent yet constantly pursues them with his mind turned outward.
Having become servants to desire, all those with desires are servants to everyone;
but one who is free from desire, having been abandoned by desire itself—whose servant could he be?
The mockery of karma is like a bamboo vessel that remains empty even when filled with hundreds of jars.
O virtuous one, how is it that the web of ritual actions does not lead to dispassion?
From the beginning of Brahmā’s day until today, alas, the transmigrating being has performed all his activities for not even a single moment without falling into anxiety.
The supreme misfortune for men is subsisting on the alms of others;
how then can subsisting on the alms of one's own son be considered good fortune?
Addressing the funeral cake with the word "dead" on the anniversary of death, [the father thinks]:
"The son will give this to the dead; what then is better than immortality? (NBs 4.7.4)
Having learned from the scriptures that one encounters hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death, do not become a consumer of the offerings of the faithful.
Long life leads to the experience of old age; abundant wealth to misery;
sons to the suffering of strife—in this saṃsāra, suffering is truly extraordinary.
He beholds the shadow of his own body, yet he is deluded by pride regarding his wealth;
he pursues his wife with passionate attachment, and truly knows not the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
In the meeting of travelers, where arrivals and departures are unexpected, attachment to one's cattle, children, wife, and so forth is not considered equal [to that felt for others]. (NBs 4.7.8)
Our teachers are truly the best among grammarians, for they,
having prescribed equanimity in place of possessiveness, bring it about.
They will surely abandon you, and you too shall abandon them;
since there is great happiness in their abandonment, what effort is there in abandoning them?
The sequence consisting of praise and blame for those deluded by worldly conventions also ends with that very body; and how many days does the body itself endure?
On one hand, all the worlds pull at the string of objects according to their respective strengths; on the other, this single, powerful Time swallows it up.
Fortune is fickle, we are fickle, and the functions of the senses are fickle;
what happiness is there, my dear, where even life itself is in doubt?
Grief, delusion, fear, dejection, mental anguish, physical disease, hunger, thirst—these and various other such sufferings constitute the brief enumeration [of suffering]. (NB 4.7.14)
[Page 66] Inquiry into Dharma: Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Dharma; Dharma is declared to be fourfold.
The obligatory, the occasional, the optional, and expiatory rites, in that order. // NBs_5,1.1 //

Those practices pertaining to the castes and stages of life, as well as purification, bathing, and so forth, which are necessary, must be performed regularly; for by not performing them, one incurs transgression.
Those [acts] which have place, time, and specific causes as their conditions are known as "contingent" (naimittika),
such as bathing, giving gifts, ancestral rites (śrāddha), recitation (japa), and so forth, on the occasion of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) or an eclipse (grahaṇa).
Dharmas consisting of expiation, such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, are performed with desire for their fruits;
they are not prescribed for one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*).
The desire for the grace of Hari, the longing for purity of mind,
and the yearning for liberation— this desire is no [ordinary] desire at all.
Therefore, those who desire liberation should perform bathing, giving, recitation, and so forth, as well as devotion to sacred fords, vows, and austerities, with that same intention.
Regarding the determination of actions, Mādhava has thus stated in the Gītā:
"In every way, obligatory duty must never be abandoned by one who seeks liberation. (NBs 5.1.7)

Even when knowledge has arisen, that which is the renunciation of latent impressions (vāsanā) for the sake of favoring the world must not be abandoned; for that indeed is the true renunciation of action (karma).
There is no abandonment of actions; rather, the renunciation of action consists of the mind.
For the wise, sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the means of purification.

Through action, there may be purification of the mind; through that, an intense desire for liberation arises. From that, through discernment, liberation occurs. [Objection: But how can that action be abandoned?
But those, dear son, who have attained through awakening that state which transcends karma, they are not servants of ritual injunction; therefore, let them move about according to their own will.
Devotion to asceticism has been practiced through deceit by those who are intent upon hypocrisy, greed, and self-aggrandizement.
Whether in a marketplace or in the middle of a city, that austerity is considered the lowest.
That asceticism which is performed according to the rules prescribed in the Vedic scriptures by one who endures cold, heat, and so forth,
yet preceded by desire, is indeed middling.
For one who is devoted to the ultimate truth and desires to know reality, that austerity which is performed without desire for the sake of restraining the mind is considered the highest.
One should offer a welcome to those who arrive and should not restrain those who depart;
one should endure everything as it comes—this is the most excellent of all ascetic practices.
The establishment of vows consists in the avoidance of others' wives, the property of others, and malice toward others.
The abandonment of passion and hatred is the supreme vow among all vows.
As it is said in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
"Averse to the wives of others, the wealth of others, and malice toward others, even the Gaṅgā says: 'When will he come and purify me? (NBs 5.3.2)
An investigation into outward appearance:
there is no liberation in a mass of matted hair, nor in saffron robes, nor in shaving the head.
Neither in ashes, nor in a patched garment, nor in a sectarian mark, nor in a water-pot.
Out of hatred, one strikes at a snake; it is a useless beating of an anthill.
Without restraint of the mind, shaving the body is in vain.
If one who is free from passion wears matted hair, a patched garment, and so forth for the sake of pacifying mental distraction, that is indeed the most excellent of all.
In the *Maunamīmāṃsā*,
silence is said to be fourfold: vocal silence (*vāṅmauna*) is the restraint of speech.
The restraint of the organs of cognition is declared to be the silence of the senses.
The restraint of the organs of action is "silence like a log" (kāṣṭhamauna), which is like a piece of wood;
but silence is also of three secondary kinds, while the dissolution of the mind is the supreme [silence].
A silent sage is not one who has become mute, nor is a silent sage a suckling infant;
nor is a silent sage merely one intent on a vow; a silent sage is one whose mind is fully withdrawn.
According to the established rules of grammar, *mauna* is the state of being a sage (*muni*).
When the state of being a sage does not exist, then *mauna* is meaningless.
The knowledge of giving is threefold: the gift of fame, the gift of desire, and the gift of compassion.
Better than each of these, and superior to them all, is the supreme dedication to Kṛṣṇa.
This is the true nature of sacred sites: "This is a sacred site," "This is a sacred site," "From here is a sacred site," and "Beyond this is another."
A sacred site much further than this has been seen by me, but not by you.
"The fruit of your pilgrimage is small, while the fruit of my pilgrimage is great"—
those who wander through sacred sites with such thoughts are deluded, but they are not true seekers of the sacred.
The destruction of sins occurs through bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha); a sacred ford is the company of the virtuous;
at a sacred ford there should be discourse on dispassion; and a sacred ford is the worship of the Lord.
"The ability to endure cold and heat is a holy ford; conduct free from attachment is a holy ford.
Those who know this as the holy ford are indeed the knowers of the true nature of the holy ford.
Skill in conduct is propriety; lack of conduct is impurity; and excessive conduct is folly.
The conjunction of reflection and conduct is the defining characteristic of right conduct.
The Determination of the Abandonment of Passion:
Those who possess wealth are not dispassionate; those who are naked are not dispassionate.
Those who are intensely attached to their own position are, in my view, considered to be devoid of passion [for the truth].
Thieves abandon their own homes out of fear alone, not out of awakening;
paramours abandon their own homes out of passion alone, not out of awakening. (NBs 6.2)
One who is angry abandons his own home due to opposition from an adversary;
one who is obstructed abandons his own home due to that very obstruction, not out of awakening.
Having attained the bliss of non-attachment through some playful exercise of awakening,
sages abandon their homes, or householders remain in the world.
As it has been said:
"What can a fool abandon? Or what fruit is there in the renunciation of one whose mind is distracted?
Let the wise man perform action or not; he is not defiled by renunciation."
Having thus reached this certainty through the teachings of those who possess the knowledge of non-duality,
the sage, indifferent toward the renunciation of passion, sports on the far shore beyond words.
Thus, this is the determination regarding the abandonment of passion for those engaged in yoga;
for, according to the definitive conclusion of the Vedānta, that [reality] is to be known by one who is in the very act of abandoning.
[Page 88–] Examination of Authority:
Many kinds of phenomena have been taught in the treatise for those who hold authority over phenomena.
In that regard, the intense desire for liberation itself constitutes the primary qualification for liberation.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, one who desires heaven has the qualification; in marriage, one who desires a son;
in trade, one who possesses greed; and for liberation, one who seeks release. (NBs 7.2)
If there is an intense desire for liberation yet dullness of wisdom persists,
one should first dispel that by means of discussions with those who know the true scriptures.
If there exists a desire for liberation, this person has no entitlement to the Vedas;
therefore, he should engage in inquiry by means of listening to the Purāṇas and other such practices. (NBs 7.4)

Whatever is stated in the Veda is indeed the same as that which is in the Purāṇa; however, the conclusion reached in the Bhāṣya is that not even a single syllable of the Veda should be recited [to the uninitiated].
Action performed according to one's qualification succeeds;
otherwise, the accomplishment of the task will not arise, and there will be great transgression.
[92] O dear one, when the mind is gladdened by the nectar of association with the virtuous, that nectar of association with the virtuous—
When that is ascertained, my liberation from delusion will occur.
For among all means of accomplishment, association with the virtuous is the most excellent;
by the perfection of this alone, every means of accomplishment is indeed perfected.
Those who are eternally devoted to the Lord, dispassionate, impartial in vision, virtuous,
and proficient in the scriptures of liberation— such persons should be served.
By the mere sight of whom faith in liberation increases, and by the play of whose speech doubt is dispelled. (NBs 8.4)
The determination of the intended meaning is achieved through the indicators of intention, such as the opening statements and so forth;
the systematic arrangement of the meanings of the scriptures is established by way of both the particular and the general.

Entering the path to liberation without contradicting the Vedas and the Śāstras, a thorough knowledge of the traditions, and the definitive determination of differences between philosophical systems. // NBs_8.6 //
Those virtuous ones who obtain knowledge from the words of both the preceding and subsequent positions— those wise ones who act as helmsmen are indeed to be served.
And so it is said in the Gītā:
"Know that through prostration, through inquiry, and through service;
the wise who have seen reality will instruct you in that knowledge. (Gītā 4.34)
The eloquence of systematic concord is to be plunged into especially; it is the eloquence of systematic concord.
By which there may arise the washing away of the mud known as the divergence of opinions.
The word, the meaning of the word, the meaning of the sentence, the [philosophical] principles, the restraint of the mind,
and the realization of the meaning of the Great Sentence— these are indeed the means of accomplishment in their proper sequence.
I shall explain, in brief and exactly as it is, the application of all those tantras therein, each according to its proper place. (NBs 9.3)

Through the science of grammar, the highest proficiency in words is produced; and proficiency in the meanings of those words is achieved through the teachings of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika systems. (NBs 9.4)
Through Mīmāṃsā, the comprehension of the meaning of sentences is perfected;
through Sāṃkhya, the manifestation of the principles [of reality]; and through Yoga, the restraint of the mind.
"The realization of the meaning of the great sayings is attained through the Vedāntas and steadfastness in Brahman";
thus, in this way, all systems of thought are in complete harmony with Brahman alone.
[Page 98–] Since non-contradiction arises as a consequence, the understanding of non-contradiction is also investigated here.
In conventional discourse, the existence of duality is equal in both the dualist and the non-dualist systems.

And since there is no contradiction in both systems regarding the fact that [the world] is imagined through non-duality, let them continue to debate repeatedly, out of their passion for disputation. (NBs 10.2)
The restraints (yamas) consist of non-violence, truthfulness, and so forth; the observances (niyamas) consist of purity and the like.
One should remain in a comfortable posture, and there should be withdrawal of the senses from all objects.
Retention, as well as meditation and the concentration of the mind—
this sevenfold limb of yoga is indeed approved by all.
Whether in Mantra, Haṭha, the Royal [Yoga], Devotion, Sāṃkhya, or the doctrine of Hari,
there is a unity of intent among all those wise ones who have entered the path to liberation.
For those who rely on forceful methods (*haṭha*), the exertion of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) alone is superior;
yet for whom is stability of mind during breath control not approved? (NBs 10.6)
Therefore, there is no difference whatsoever in the views of those who speak of liberation;
yet, even among the Vedāntins, there exists some slight difference in their opinions.
The application of the Sāṃkhya collyrium-stick should be performed as an ointment for the eyes with that Sāṃkhya collyrium-stick.
Then, through the destruction of darkness, a subtle object is perceived.
Devahūti was enlightened by Kapila Mukunda through the discernment of all principles; that is what is called Sāṃkhya.

There exists a certain indefinable primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), from which all transformations—whether gross or subtle, moving or stationary—originate. (NBs 11.3)

The Great Principle (mahat-tattva), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātrakāṇi)—these seven indeed constitute both the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikṛti). (NBs 11.4)
That which is a modification of its own causes is the "nature" (prakṛti) of that which arises from it. Thus, there are eight natures; from these, the modifications (vikṛti) come into being.
The five elements beginning with space, the five faculties of cognition, and the five faculties of action, together with the mind, constitute the sixteen [principles]. (NBs 11.6)
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth are called the pentad of elements;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities respectively.
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the organs of cognition;
and speech, hands, feet, the anus, and so forth are the five organs of action.
The mind (*manas*) consists of both [the self and the non-self], and by that [addition], twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) are proclaimed;
indeed, the entire triple world is a transformation of those [principles].
Because primordial nature (prakṛti) consists of the three qualities (guṇas), everything indeed consists of the three qualities;
for the qualities of passion (rajas), purity (sattva), and darkness (tamas) have red, white, and black forms respectively.
Rajas is considered mobile, tamas is stagnant, and sattva is regarded as luminous;
indeed, tamas is the lowest, rajas is the middle, and sattva is the highest.
Greed and the like are states of *rajas*; dullness and the like are states of *tamas*;
and happiness, clarity, and awareness are proclaimed to be states of *sattva*.
The gods and so forth are of the nature of sattva; humans and so forth are recorded as being of the nature of rajas;
animals, elemental beings, and so forth are of the nature of tamas—thus let everything be discerned.
Qualities that are mutually contradictory, yet act as both allies and causes for one another, perform their functions when combined, despite their discordant activities. (NBs 11.14)
The entire universe consists of the qualities (guṇas), whereas the Self is indeed devoid of qualities;
yet, by virtue of being the illuminator, it appears as if it has entered therein.
Just as the tongue, situated among the thirty-two teeth, knows tastes and perceives flavors,
so too does the knower of one's own self know the principles within the twenty-four principles.
Māyā, greedy for sense objects, makes her own single Lord assume many forms and sports with him, just like a courtesan.
For, having joined with the Puruṣa in a state of non-separation,
Nature (Prakṛti) causes him to dance by means of her various forms.
The Lord is faultless and immovable, while the bride is faulty and fickle;
between these two spouses, there will surely be a disruption of aesthetic flavor.
Having been thoroughly understood as distinct and also as having a wicked nature,
she, being modest, does not show her face and even dies.
Neither primordial nature nor its transformation is the Puruṣa; he is of an immovable nature, whose very essence is pure and enlightened—such is the definitive conclusion of the Sāṃkhya.
In the *Yogadīkṣācintāmaṇi*, the Pātañjala Yoga:
Now, therefore, the *Cintāmaṇi* of the initiation into yoga (*yogadīkṣā*) is proclaimed.
Through the attainment of that, the poverty of non-enlightenment is entirely destroyed.
Śambhu is the great lord of yoga; Hari is the great lord of yoga;
Brahmā is the great lord of yoga; and Bhavānī is the perfected yoginī.
Sanaka and others, Vasiṣṭha and others, Kaca, Datta, Śuka and others,
as well as Arundhatī and others, attained perfection through yoga.
The yoga that consists in the union of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (parātman) through self-knowledge—that is yoga;
because it is the cause of that [union], various kinds of yoga are recognized.
According to the principle of contradictory characteristics, "Bhadraka" (the Auspicious) refers to that which is inauspicious;
however, Keśava has stated that "yoga" is the dissociation from all suffering.
Even for a mind that is extremely fickle, immobility may arise through the power of yoga, just as it does for the great mountain Vindhya.
And so Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"Having established the ethereal concentration (nābhasī dhāraṇā), I remain free from all feverish distress until the Lotus-born One again engages in the work of creation."
The cessation of the fluctuations of the mind is considered the primary [yoga] in the system of Patañjali;
however, the cessation of the fluctuations of the vital breath is secondary, because it is a means to that end.

In this regard, the Sūtra states: "The eight limbs are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi).
Restraint consists of non-stealing, truthfulness, non-violence, celibacy, and non-possessiveness."
The observances (niyama) are purity, contentment, austerity, study, and dedication to the Lord.
Posture is considered to be the stability of the body in a state of comfort;
breath control is the restraint of the vital breath through the techniques of retention (*kumbhaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the restraint of the restless senses;
dhāraṇā (concentration) is considered to be the fixing of the mind upon a particular location.
The uninterrupted flow of the mind toward the object of meditation is called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption).
The eighth stage, *samādhi* (concentration), should be known as abiding in that very state through identification with it.
For that meditative absorption (samādhi) is indeed twofold: it is both conscious (saṃprajñāta) and its other [unconscious].
Furthermore, there are five external limbs beginning with restraint (yama), and then another set of internal limbs.
Conscious absorption (samprajñāta-samādhi) is fourfold, being permeated by vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, and asmitā.
That in which nothing whatsoever is cognized is called "non-cognitive" (asaṃprajñāta).
It is of two kinds: that which has existence as its condition and that which has the means [of yoga] as its condition.
Even for the deluded, the dissolution of the mind may occur through the firmness of ascetic practice;
that occurs either in primordial nature (prakṛti) or in the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva), and it is indeed based on worldly existence (bhava).
Just as the body of Hiraṇyakaśipu, who desired sovereignty over the three worlds,
was devoured by worms and covered even by an anthill.
Preceded by faith, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, and the abandonment of desire,
that dissolution of the mind is the means-condition for the Lords of Sages.
It has been stated that for those whose minds have strayed and who desire to attain composure,
there is austerity, the recitation of the Vedas, and the dedication of all actions to Hari.
There exists a certain unique Person, the Lord, who is entirely untouched by afflictions, karma, and their various results, as well as by the latent dispositions based upon them.
He is omniscient by nature, and the *praṇava* is its designator;
therefore, this recitation of it, preceded by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is the means to liberation.
Just as there is disease, its cause, the medicine, and health,
medical treatment is fourfold according to the distinction of those factors to be analyzed.
The suffering of birth, as well as delusion, consciousness, and liberation—
through the distinction of these objects to be analyzed, the Yoga-śāstra is fourfold.
The non-discrimination between the Spirit (puruṣa) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti) is that delusion which is the cause of suffering;
it perishes through the awakening to the knowledge of their equality and their difference.
For one who is intent on the practice of yoga, supernatural powers that bestow enjoyments may arise;
however, no regard should be paid to them, since they are considered obstacles.

The various types of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) that have been described as resulting from the diversity of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) have not been examined here, because they are of absolutely no utility [for the goal of this treatise].
The Śaiva Yoga;
the Yoga of Śiva is now being described.
Mantra, Laya, Haṭha, and Rājayoga: yoga is fourfold.
The mantra-yogas are the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa, the twelve-syllable mantra of Vāsudeva,
and the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Rāma, and Gopāla; these are praised in the Tāpinī Upaniṣad.
The five-syllabled mantra of Śiva is the most excellent, and the Dakṣiṇāmūrtti [mantra] is the highest;
for ascetics, however, the Great Saying (mahāvākya) and likewise the solitary Praṇava [are supreme].
These and other great mantras, perfected through such procedures as the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*),
are considered to bestow liberation immediately by the grace of the deity.
[Page 137] Haṭhayoga:
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one should seek the ascetic maiden (bālaraṇḍā).
One should seize that supreme state of Viṣṇu by means of forceful exertion.
In this regard, Gorakṣa says:
"This is the ladder to liberation, this is the deception of Time:
that the mind, having turned away from enjoyment, is attached to the Supreme Self. (NBs 12.3.2)
If there is supreme detachment, if one’s diet is as prescribed,
and if one dwells constantly in solitude, then Haṭhayoga is not difficult to attain.
However, this [attainment] is obtained through the initiations of the Guru and not otherwise;
in its transgression there is great fault, while in its attainment there is great merit.
Forceful yoga (haṭha) of infinite extent was taught by the Enemy of Tripura; however, its essence is the threefold bond, for through that alone is perfection attained.
At the base there is the root-lock (mūlabandha), in the middle there is the uḍḍiyāna-lock, and at the throat the jālandhara-lock; by these, the vital wind becomes perfected.
Having entered the Suṣumṇā through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by means of Kuṇḍalinī,
Śakti resides in the root-place (mūlasthāna), while Sadāśiva resides in the place of Brahmā (brahmasthāna).
The Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows liberation upon yogins;
by the mere intention of it, one is released from all sins.
The first wheel is the Ādhāra, and likewise the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
Maṇipūra shall be the third, and the fourth is Anāhata.
Purity is the fifth wheel, while the sixth is the wheel of command (ājñācakra).
The seventh is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); for that is indeed the cave of the bee.

Having firmly placed the foot joined at the root of the thigh in the position of the womb (yoni-sthānaka), and having made the body perfectly level and motionless, one should remain with the senses restrained like a pillar, gazing at the space between the eyebrows with a steady gaze; this is called Siddhāsana, which effects the breaking open of the door to liberation.
Having joined the hands in the *sampuṭita* gesture and firmly assumed the *siddhāsana*, placing the chin tightly against the chest, one should then fix the mind in meditation;

repeatedly drawing the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) upward and holding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one gradually releases it while awakening [the *kuṇḍalinī*], whereby the awakening of the power (*śakti*) occurs.
Grasping the serpent by its tail, the wise man should awaken it;
having abandoned sleep, that power rises up forcefully.
For one whose vital breath has ascended and who has abandoned all karma without exception,
the innate state arises spontaneously through yoga.
O Goddess, as long as the vital breath has not perished, knowledge arises within the mind while the mind still lives; but when the mind dies, the vital breath ceases.
When these two—the vital breath and the mind—both reach dissolution, that person attains liberation; never anyone else.

When the yogi exists with his mind and breath dissolved into the internal object, looking outward with a gaze of motionless pupils—though seeing this external world, he does not see it; this indeed is the divine Śāmbhavī Mudrā. Through the grace of the Guru, he seeks the state of Śambhu, the reality that is distinct from both void and non-void.
When the function of the vital breath has dissolved, the function of the mind dissolves;
through Haṭhayoga, the union of Śiva and Śakti arises.
Indeed, by the grace of Haṭhayoga, those such as Gorakṣa and Carpaṭi,
having evaded the rod of Time, wander throughout the universe.
Having fixed the mind within the *śakti* and the *śakti* within the midst of the mind,
the practitioners of *haṭhayoga* effect the union of Śiva and Śakti.
The Prowess of Śiva’s Power:
Now I shall describe the prowess of Śiva’s power under the guise of a hymn of praise.
When [reality] has been purified by subtle vision, one should become free from wonder regarding it.
I meditate upon that Power of the Supreme Self, who is indeed dual in form, whose nature is both dual and non-dual, and who is ultimately non-dual in form.
I bow to that wondrous power, which remains undetermined as to who she is, whose she is, from where, by whom, for whom, toward whom, where, how, or when.
Śiva is the agent, Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is the knower, and Śiva is the Lord;
I bow to that wondrous Śakti, who is merely His subordinate.
I bow to that wondrous Śakti, for whom Śiva is merely the witness, while she herself is the agent, the enjoyer, the knower, and the sovereign.
I bow to that wondrous Śakti, who abides as the very particularity within the Great God (Mahādeva) through her own particularity, and who is known by means of those very particularities.
I bow to that wondrous Śakti, who, while abiding as possessing characteristics within the Great God who possesses characteristics, is herself known through those very characteristics.
I bow to that wondrous Śakti, who, while abiding as distinct from the Great God who is Himself beyond characteristics, is known through those very same distinctions.
I bow to that wondrous power, which, because its nature is neither consciousness nor unconsciousness, remains as if insentient, yet serves as the cause of sentience within consciousness.
"I am caused to will by the will"—thus [consciousness] appears in its conceptualized nature; yet in pure consciousness, the cause of willing is that wondrous power (śakti) which I revere.
What can one who lacks power accomplish?
I bow to that wondrous Power by which Śiva is empowered. (NBs 12.4.11)
Indeed, power is certainly capable in its functions when it resides in one who possesses power;
yet, without relying on Śiva, it is powerless. I bow to that wondrous Power.
Since neither power nor the possessor of power possesses substantial reality in the non-conceptual state, I salute that wondrous Power which has attained a state of equilibrium within Śiva.
When the supreme power of Śiva has been cultivated in this way by those who possess the nature of such cultivation,
the ocean of the essence of aesthetic rapture (*sāmarasya*) spontaneously wells up within their own hearts.

I meditate upon that wondrous power of Śiva, which consists of devotion in the devotee, of animality in the beast, of knowledge in the learned, of Brahman in the creation, of Hari in the maintenance, and prior to the kalpa, of pure consciousness; which consists of mental modifications in the individual soul, of insentience in the inert, and which, in the state beyond the highest, consists of the play of its own bliss.

Having abandoned even those pleasures of the senses with intense devotion—those fragments of bliss sought after by the dull-witted who desire material gain—I worship the Blessed One, whose form is bliss, who flows with the nectar of bliss, who is the pinnacle of the limit of bliss, and who is proclaimed in the authoritative scriptures of the *Ānandopaniṣad*. 12.4.16.
In *layayoga*,
the flickering mind indeed does not know the bliss of immobility.
In order to contemplate that [reality], dissolution was shown to him by the sages.
Indeed, Śambhu has described to Gaurī countless sequences of dissolution;
by whom could they be known, and by whom could they be described? Nevertheless, I shall tell you something.

At the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking, and at the end of sleep and at the onset of waking, there occurs the dissolution (laya) of the mind; therein, one should practice reflection upon the Self.
When the self becomes relaxed, like a porter who has laid down his burden, then indeed one should perform the worship of Śiva with devotion.
Whenever the mind becomes lax, at that very moment Maheśāna should be contemplated; that indeed is the worship of Śiva.
Because one contemplates all desired and undesired states as being solely desirable,
that very state of freedom from attachment and aversion in the mind is itself the worship of Śiva.
Affliction itself is the supreme worship, just as the pressing of the feet [is a service];
suffering alone is the highest worship, just as a rough massage [is a service].
Fatigue itself is the supreme worship; in fatigue, the mind dissolves into consciousness.
Indeed, fear is the supreme worship, according to the Vedic revelation: "From Him [comes] terror. (NBs 12.5.8)
Giving is indeed the supreme worship when it is offered to the Supreme Self;
yet non-giving is the supreme worship if the mind becomes serene.
Disease itself is the supreme worship, since through disease the destruction of evil occurs;
health is the supreme worship, for freedom from illness is the means to liberation.
Indeed, all that is performed for the sake of Śiva is the supreme ritual worship;
yet non-action itself is the highest worship, being unwavering and consisting of meditative absorption.
Association with the virtuous is the supreme worship; association with the virtuous is the means to liberation.
Association with the non-virtuous is the highest form of worship, wherein delusion is examined.
Fortitude is indeed the supreme worship, for the steadfast one partakes of the immortal;
lack of fortitude is the supreme worship, through the swift liberation from what must be done.
Praise alone is the supreme worship; the deity is pleased by praise.
Yet, for those who are like the veins of a friend, even censure is the highest form of worship.
Craving alone is the supreme worship, for it desires much for the sake of the gods;
contentment is the supreme worship, for the god has the characteristic of contentment.
For this circumambulation is the supreme pilgrimage and the supreme worship of the God;
a seat is the supreme worship, and a comfortable seat is the highest yoga.
Eating is the supreme worship in the form of an offering to the deity;
not eating is the highest worship, for Hari is fond of fasting.
Remaining steadfast is the supreme worship; that is one's own attendance upon [the deity].
Falling down is the supreme worship, consisting in the very nature of prostration.
Speaking is the supreme worship of Hari, for everything consists of praise;
yet silence is the supreme worship, for that silence is his very exposition.
Action itself is the supreme worship, for it proceeds from that [supreme reality] as its manifestation;
indeed, non-action is the highest worship—“remain in silence,” says the Vedic word.
Birth itself is the supreme worship; that is the descent of the existent Hari.
Living is the supreme worship; while living, one should accomplish one's duties.
For a long-lived yogin, the supreme worship is longevity;
for one of short life, the supreme worship is immediate liberation from this [world].
Death is the supreme worship, taking the form of the discarding of the used flower offering;
for sorrow is indeed the supreme worship, as sorrow is the means for achieving dispassion.
Joy itself is the supreme worship, for Hari is always of a joyful nature;
nourishment is the highest worship, for one who is well-composed in mind is truly nourished.
Emaciation is the supreme honor, for the limbs of yogins are indeed emaciated;
gain is the supreme honor, for gain is the cause of contentment.
The supreme honor is indeed the absence of pride; from that alone one is liberated.
Excellence itself is the supreme honor; the virtuous person is esteemed by the good.
Since freedom from egoism is itself the highest worship of faults,
pride itself is the highest worship, for by it the Supreme Lord is honored.
Disrespect is the highest honor; through such lack of pride, the yogi attains perfection.
For wealth is indeed the highest honor, and wealth is the means for accomplishing dharma.
Poverty is the highest honor, for Brahman is attained by those who possess nothing;
vigilance is the highest honor, for it is through vigilance that one achieves perfection.
Negligence is the supreme worship, for through it one forgets what ought to be done;
deep sleep is the supreme worship, for that is indeed the meditative absorption (samādhi) of yogins.
The yoga of action is the supreme worship: it is the dedication of action to Brahma in Hari.
The yoga of devotion is the supreme worship: he who is my devotee is dear to me.
The yoga of knowledge is the supreme worship; through knowledge, one attains absolute liberation.
The fourth [state] is the highest worship, whose very nature is direct realization.
Listening is the supreme worship, for the Supreme Lord is heard;
reflection is the supreme worship, for reflection is the means to meditation.
If some teacher who resembles my own guru should touch one's ear,
then all that worship becomes the very form of absorption into the Divine.
For all types of absorption as well, the pursuit of *nāda* is supreme because it is the cause of the forgetting of the universe; for *nāda* is indeed the highest absorption.
Just as a bee drinking nectar does not long for the fragrance,
so the mind attached to the sound [of the breath] does not long for sense objects.
Now listen to the Elixir of Devotion, the essence of all established doctrines— the Elixir of Devotion.
That is the elixir which is the medicine for birth, death, old age, and disease.
Devotion is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as knowledge, dispassion, and the purification of the internal organ.
That attachment by which this individual soul attains the nature of Brahman—
having been accomplished by Sanaka and others— is designated as "bhakti."
If all the requirements for practice are present but devotion is absent,
then the fulfillment of those requirements is as futile as threshing chaff.
If there is no other means [of accomplishment], but devotion exists toward Maheśvara,
then detachment, knowledge, and liberation will be achieved gradually.
For no one would be liberated without the grace of the Lord;
liberation occurs solely through the grace of the Lord—this is the certainty.
The Lord, being perfectly complete, does not depend upon anything;
rather, being swiftly pleased by mere devotion, He bestows supreme grace.
May that unswerving affection which the undiscriminating have for sense-objects not depart from my heart as I remember you.
If there is devotion characterized by love toward the Supreme Self, the Lord of the Universe, then everything is accomplished; nothing remains to be done.
That direct experience which is described in the Vedāntas is indeed the very transformation of devotion characterized by love.
The meaning of the scripture was fully understood, and love for Maheśvara arose;
through the manifestation of the bliss of that love, duality vanished from memory.
Everything consists of Vāsudeva; the world has Vāsudeva as its very self.
For one who is thus enriched by the essence of non-duality, what knowledge remains?
Vāsudeva is the supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without.
"Minute, vast, lean, stout, possessing qualities, devoid of qualities, the Great One"—with such words as these, the Vaiṣṇava devotee praises Keśava. (NBs 13.14)
Śiva is the creator, Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is the Lord of all lords;
Śiva is the Self, Śiva is the individual soul—nothing other than Śiva exists.
And Śambhu praises Śaṅkara as the Eight-formed One (Aṣṭamūrti) by means of his eight forms: ether, wind, fire, water, earth, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the sun, and the moon. NBs_13.16.
When this love has reached its full development, it is indeed knowledge itself.
Now, another argument follows:
a child addresses his father, saying, "Father, Father."
But he does not know anything at all regarding the meaning of the word "father."
When he gradually attains proficiency in the meaning of the word "father," then he indeed reaches the certain conviction that "this one is truly my father."
Thus, a devotee who worships the God according to the procedures taught in the Vedas and scriptures attains supreme realization and becomes liberated in due course.
Furthermore, a difference in characteristics is indeed the cause for a difference in entities;
however, no difference in characteristics is observed in the scriptures between the devotee and the person of knowledge.
Dispassion, reflection, purity, restraint of the senses,
and supreme delight in the Veda— this is the single characteristic of both.
In this chapter titled "The Yoga of Devotion," that which was declared as the definition of devotion in eight verses has been observed by me among the knowers. (NBs 13.22)
"One worships [the deity] saying 'I am yours,' while another says 'I am indeed you';
despite this slight difference, the transformation is the same for both. (NBs 13.23)
When a devotee of the Divine perceives the God both within and without,
contemplating "I am His servant," he forgets even the form of the syllable *Dā*.
That has been observed among those of single-minded devotion, headed by Nārada;
I shall speak of a certain distinction therein—listen with an attentive mind.
If a devotee relishes God, then the wise man likewise relishes God;
although both share the same flavor, they are nevertheless slightly distinct.
The Buddhas have become devoid of any other flavor than the essence of awakening;
likewise, devotees never possess a flavor of affection that exceeds [that for the Buddha].
Now, the objection: Indeed, there is no liberation without knowledge even by means of a hundred arguments;
likewise, there is no knowledge without devotion even by means of a hundred methods. (NBs 13.28)
"From devotion comes knowledge, and from that, liberation—this is the common sequence.
However, Vasiṣṭha and others were knowers [of reality], while Nārada and others were indeed devotees. (NBs 13.29)
What cause for this kind of systematic arrangement should be investigated?
To this it is said: listen to that which is the manifold cause. (NBs 13.30)
I shall speak with an illustration so that the meaning may become clear:
for indeed, the destruction of both suffering and sin occurs through bathing in the Gaṅgā.
For one who seeks the pacification of suffering, there shall also be the destruction of evil;
and for one who seeks the pacification of evil, their suffering likewise perishes.
The destruction of heat and evil, and bathing—these three are equal for both;
nevertheless, one seeks coolness, while the second seeks purity.
Just as there was a difference in their names due to a difference in their states,
in the very same way, those wise ones by whom the Lord was resorted to for the sake of liberation [attained that goal].
Indeed, those wise ones who have attained knowledge through devotion and are thus liberated are truly the knowers;
while those who, weary of worldly existence, have taken refuge in Hari for the sake of devotion [are also such].
Then, through the power of devotion, knowledge arises from one's own nature;
those who, having attained that knowledge, are liberated, are described as "devotees. (NBs 13.36)
Dispassion, devotion, realization, and liberation are indeed the same for both;
nevertheless, due to a difference in their inner disposition (*bhāva*), there arose a difference in their names. (NBs 13.37)
For the knower, liberation is the primary fruit, while devotion is secondary because it is the means to that;
for the devotee, devotion itself is primary, and liberation occurs as a secondary consequence.
O wise one, by this method as well, devotion to the Lord is supreme;
furthermore, that other glory is the Supreme Self, Hari himself, whose nature is supreme bliss.
Placing devotion to Śiva at the forefront, Sanaka and others, Vasiṣṭha and others, Nandi, Skanda, Śuka, and others, partake of the elixir of the flavor of devotion.
Even those who have attained that state enjoy the elixir of devotion;
as for the question, "How can there be devotion without duality? hear the answer to that.

Duality exists for the sake of delusion prior to awakening; once awakening is attained through the intellect, duality is imagined for the sake of devotion—and even from the perspective of non-duality, duality is more beautiful.
And so it is said in the Bhāgavata:
"Even sages who delight in the Self and are free from all bonds offer causeless devotion to the One of Vast Strides; such are the qualities of Hari. (NBs 13.43)
When the bliss of the equality of flavors has arisen, even duality is like nectar,
as between two friends or between a husband and wife— the individual self and the supreme self.
She dwells in his heart with affection and feels bashful according to worldly custom,
like a bride who is eternally joyful and full of wonder.
Ultimate non-duality exists for the sake of resorting to duality;
if such devotion exists, it is indeed superior to a hundred liberations.
Whether the beloved plays according to the manner of love within the heart of the most dear one, or whether the beloved performs service at the pair of feet;
or whether one who has realized the truth sports in non-conceptual samādhi, or indeed in the practice of worship—surely those two are exactly equal.
The Lord of the Universe should be worshipped with a feeling accompanied by devotion by the wise woman, even when their difference has dissolved;
the Lord of her life should be gazed upon by the clever woman with a glance veiled by the hem of her garment, even though their hearts have met.
Now, a verse based on the aesthetic sentiment of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*):

In yoga there is no access, nor in the practice of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), which is difficult to conceive; these two—pertaining to this world and the next—are forever shunned by a mind devoid of flavor.
Yet some cowherd has been made our friend, and he, moreover, is in the company of many women; even sages seek his station—what could be more wonderful than this? (NBs 13.49)
This body is thrilled with horripilation; the mind is gladdened by devotion; tears of love adorn the face; and the voice in the throat is faltering.
For us who perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa, there is not even a moment’s respite. Is this fourfold liberation now fluttering at our door, as if eager for service?
Our desire for you is intense, yet you have no taste for anything other than devotion; our delight is incomparable in bowing at your very feet.
While we are full of longing, you are suddenly free from desire; when we have attained your state, we become free from longing—this is your greatness, O Hari, which bestows liberation upon us.
In the *Rājayoga*, from the section on the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmikā*) up until the conclusion of the work, there is the *Bhūmikābhedabhāskara*.
In this [work] on the unfathomable essence of awakening, rājayoga is set forth.
Now, this *Bhūmikābhedabhāskara* should be kept in the heart;
by its mere grace, the darkness within the heart dissolves.
There are seven stages of ignorance and likewise seven stages of knowledge:

"Waking-dream," "dream-waking," as well as "dream-sleep" and "sleep-waking"—thus delusion is sevenfold; hear now their detailed explanation. (NBs 14.1.4)
Just as every tree exists potentially within a seed stored in a granary,

One who does not become attached even to pleasant objects— namely sound, touch, smell, form, and taste—

But surely, in the concentration of the deluded, in fainting, death, and deep sleep, as well as in the fourth state (turiya), the splendor of the visible world is not perceived; so then, from what source does the distinction between them arise?
To this, the following is the reply:
By those who, desiring spiritual perfection, have performed great and severe austerities, even their bodies were forgotten as they were devoured by worms, insects, and the like. (NBs 15.17)
This is not fainting, nor is it disease; this is not death, for there is life here.
It is clearly not deep sleep either, because of the absence of the bliss of deep sleep. (NBs 15.18)
Because they lack the attainment of their own true nature and because of their state of delusion, there is no fourth [state] among these;
yet, the appearance of the visible does not exist in them, and by that much alone, one's purpose is not accomplished.

Even when they have emerged [from meditative absorption], as long as their cyclic existence remains as it was, so long as the vision of self does not exist, cyclic existence remains uncontradicted. (NBs 15.20)
I shall relate an illustration here; listen with an attentive mind:
what is forgotten in a dream is not sublated by the waking state, whereas [what is experienced] in the waking-dream is not sublated.
Therefore, immediately after that, just as it truly is, the dream is sublated within the waking state; by that, the dream has come to be recognized as false. (NBs 15.22)
Likewise, in the concentration of the deluded, the entire world is forgotten;
yet after emerging from it, it subsequently exists just as it was before.
The entire universe is sublated in the fourth state; therefore, it has attained the status of being false.
Even upon emerging from that state, O dear one, for the sage it remains only false and not real.
Just as someone who, having seen a snake in a rope, has gone to another place, still fears it when he returns there again. (NBs 15.25)
If, having known "this is not a snake," one has gone to another place,
then when he returns again, he does not fear it.
Likewise, when one who has attained a state of oblivion to cyclic existence through deluded meditative absorption reaches emergence from it,
then the fear born of cyclic existence arises.
If, having attained the oblivion of saṃsāra through the meditative absorption of the wise,
he later undergoes emergence from that state, he does not fear it because [the world] has been sublated.
If liberation for an embodied being were to occur simply through forgetfulness, then since deep sleep occurs constantly, why would one not be liberated by it? (NBs 15.29)
Therefore, the fourth state is the most excellent of all and distinct from them;
even the other six states do not equal a sixteenth part of it.
Even if Garuḍa were to run with great speed for an entire kalpa of Brahmā, he would not reach it; thus, that [distance] becomes ever more distant from afar.

If there is faith in the Vedānta, if there is an intense desire for liberation, and if the practice of meditation is likewise profound, then that [liberation] is easily attainable everywhere. (NBs 15.32)
Death, fainting, and deep sleep are not austerity; therefore, they are fruitless.

Knowledge is indeed the meditative absorption of the wise, for it bestows liberation;
