“O wise one, if you say that the Supreme Self is revealed through the discernment of categories, then this is my own view as well.”
In the system of the bound and the liberated, there are not multiple selves in reality;
the Sage Gautama stated that there is only one self established as manifold.
"The complexity of conceptualization is a fault; the simplicity of conceptualization is a merit"—this very principle stated by the logicians is what pleases me.
Now follows the determination of the Sāṃkhya:
O Sāṃkhya, you have enumerated the enumerations of the principles (*tattva*).
What is the use of Sāṃkhya enumeration? Contemplate Brahman, which transcends all enumeration.
The knowledge of reality has been proclaimed by you, and that knowledge of reality is my conviction;
for it is the realization of that which transcends reality which indeed leads to liberation.
The enumeration was formulated by me for the purpose of examining the person;
if the Sāṃkhya speaks thus, then this is approved by me.
There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal.
Behold the Puruṣa, O Sāṃkhya! What is the use of calculation?
Now follows the determination of the Pātañjala system:
This diligent study of the Pātañjala [Yoga] is undertaken for the sake of attaining the perfection of yoga.
This is merely skill in the arts; for that [perfection] is indeed abiding in one's true nature.
O Yogasiddha, for living beings, the manifestation of multiple bodies (kāyavyūha) is not difficult to attain;
however, the perfection of liberation beyond the body (videhamuktatā) is not achieved through the manifestation of multiple bodies.
You consider yourself a perfected master of yoga who knows how to enter another's body;
yet you do not truly know the art of entering another's body.
Even spirits and the like know how to enter another's body;
yet that is not true accomplishment, nor is it bondage, because it is merely the act of entering a body.
If death is inevitable, then what is the use of long life?
Drink the nectar of consciousness, which destroys birth, death, and old age.
What is the use of knowing an object residing in another's mind?
Therefore, behold the Supreme Brahman, the reality established within your own mind.
If there were no hearing or seeing of one's own self situated nearby,
what accomplishment would that be which is the accomplishment of hearing and seeing from afar?
Even crows and other such creatures possess the power of moving through the sky and so forth;
yet one would not be perfected by [mundane] accomplishments. What purpose, then, is there in such accomplishments?
"Indeed, there is no perfection; for the perfection of yoga does not bring about the perfection of power, heroism, and so forth.
By this, yoga is refuted," as stated in the Vedāntabhāṣya.
"If the knower of yoga says, 'Success is the thorough knowledge of the self, whereas the [supernatural] powers are obstacles,' that is precisely our own view."
Now, the determination through investigation: if this principle that "action is painful" is held by the Mīmāṃsaka, [then...]
At that time, he himself admitted his own participation in affliction.
The Mīmāṃsaka has spoken the truth, for one who knows karma understands that karma is painful;
therefore, even for him, Brahman must be investigated in order to bring about the cessation of what is undesirable.
Birth arises from karma, and the arising of karma occurs through birth;
if this is so, how can there be liberation from birth for one who is bound by karma?
For those who maintain that awakening is primary, liberation alone is primary;
for those who maintain that karma is primary, birth alone is primary.
How can he who, due to his own dullness born of karma and his lack of qualification for sacrifices,
proclaimed [the path] as being free from desire yet consisting mostly of impurity— how can such a person be pure?
One should declare that action which has been examined as being purifying and free from desire;
for the examination of such optional (kāmya) action consists solely of suffering.
If the ritualist (karmaṭha) says, "The purification of the mind comes through actions, and through that purification, consciousness is attained," then this is exactly what I agree with.
Now follows the determination of the Dharmaśāstra:
through the investigation of the Dharmaśāstras, the Dharma of Liberation yields great fruit.
In this [practice], there is no loss of effort, nor is any obstacle found.
And so Yājñavalkya says:
"Among the acts of sacrifice, right conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts, this alone is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga."
Now follows the determination of what is based on revelation (śrauta) and what is based on tradition (smārta).
That which is heard is called śrauta, and that which is remembered is called smārta.
Hearing and reflection constitute the determination of what is derived from the Vedas and the Smṛtis.
That which has been heard from the mouths of the venerable gurus is remembered and never forgotten;
those for whom this [knowledge of] the Śrauta and Smārta rites exists are indeed the knowers of the Śrauta and Smārta.
Now, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*): grammar (*śikṣā*), ritual (*kalpa*), etymology (*nirukta*), prosody (*chandas*), and phonology (*vyākaraṇa*).
Astronomy and the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), as well as their definitive determination.
Now, the determination of training:
If that training by which one who is pure through the state of being bodiless is trained is not attained,
then what indeed has been trained by that training?
Now, the determination of the ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*): If this first of the ritual manuals were not free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), [it would not be authoritative].
What is gained by ritual manuals consisting of conceptual constructions and mental fabrications?
If that ritual procedure by which one is fit for becoming a Brahmā is not itself established as such,
then the Kalpasūtra is purposeless.
Now follows the determination of grammar: the etymological analysis of words must be sought for the sake of understanding the meaning of the great sentence.
If that very [object] is not known, then what is the use of grammar?
If that by which this universe is manifested is itself not manifested,
then what is the use of grammar for one who does not know that which is vast?
But if what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted are not understood from the treatise through the repeated use of fully established words, then what is the use of grammar?
Now, the determination of etymology (*nirukta*): etymology is the abiding of consciousness (*cit*), and etymology is the awakening of consciousness.
If one does not know that etymology, what is the use of the explanations of etymology?
Now follows the determination of meter:
if that meter is not known, by what could one sport according to one's own whim?
What is the purpose of meters endowed with *yara-staja-bhna-ma*?
Now follows the determination of astronomy (*jyautiṣa-nirṇaya*).
That by means of which the light of the sun and other luminaries shines, yet does not perceive it— [that is astronomy].
If that were so, then what would have been accomplished by that treatise on luminosity?
Now, regarding the Vedas:
first, the determination of the Ṛgveda.
"We worship you, the Self who bestows supreme bliss"—
when this has been offered, what then remains for the Universal Self regarding the *ṛc* verse of the *hautra* liturgy?
Now follows the determination of the Yajurveda: If the unborn source of progeny (*aja*) is red, white, and black;
Why was he not challenged at the sacrificial session of Brahmā by means of the *yajuṣ* of the *ādhvaryava*?
Now follows the determination of the Sāmaveda:
by means of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad and with a voice faltering with love.
If the Brahman priest does not sing with the *sāman*, then what is the use of the *udgātṛ* priest?
Now follows the determination of the Atharvaveda:
the Atharvanic knowledge of Brahman descended from the mouth of Pippalāda.
If [the Veda] does not cause wonder in the heart, what then is the fruit of the Atharva [Veda]?
Now follows the determination of Ayurveda:
If the nectar of knowledge has not been drunk, immortality is not achieved.
If death itself has already arrived, then the science of Ayurveda is useless.
Now follows the determination of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*):
by means of the bow that is the syllable *praṇava*, and the arrow that is awakening (*prabodha*).
If the target, Brahman, were not pierced, the science of archery would be useless.
Now follows the determination of the *gāndharva*:
indeed, the Self is [revealed] by the melody, the song, and the *gāndhāra* note.
If it is not like a Gandharva singing, then what has been accomplished by the art of music?
Now follows the determination of the treatise on wealth (*artha-śāstra*).
All objects of wealth are actually non-wealth; true wealth is the vision of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛk*).
If the ultimate truth is not attained, then the treatise on worldly affairs is useless.
[468] Now follows the determination of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsandhyā*):
Thus, by means of the diversion of knowledge and through curiosity for the Vedas and the Śāstras, [the day should be spent].
The entire day has passed; the evening twilight has arrived.
In the very same way, for however long one observes worldly affairs,
the subsequent reconnection with meditative absorption is known as the evening twilight (sāyaṃsandhyā).
Now follows the determination of the conventional reckoning of night:
When the day called "conventional" has passed and the pleasure of the evening twilight has been enjoyed, and night having arisen, one should set the bolts on the door-leaves with an unwavering mind.

Having now drunk to his heart's content the milk of pure awakening, which is as sweet as nectar, the youth repeatedly enjoys a certain beloved woman upon the couch named "Perfect Meditative Absorption."
When love arose for that slender-limbed young woman, who was fond of amorous play, wondrous to the mind, eternally bestowing happiness, and consisting of the sport of bliss;

he—having attained the state of the Lord of Serpents through union with his beloved, who was sporting upon his chest and embracing him as his own creative power (kalā)—became a treasure-house of happiness, the crest-jewel of the lords of yogis.
[472] Now follows the determination of the results of reflecting upon the daily conduct of the Lord of Munis.
This daily conduct of the Lord of Munis should be contemplated day by day.
By reflecting upon this for no long time, a person shall attain freedom from anxiety.

When this [pramāṇa] has been correctly understood through the reasoning concerning the relationship between the probandum and the probans, as well as the result and the refinement [of the means], nothing remains to be known.
This daily routine of the Lord of Sages is difficult even for the lords of sages to describe;
may the Lord of Pārvatī forgive my loquacity therein.
The *Nirañjanapañcāśatkam* is that in which the Vedāntas and the experience of the wise are the authority.
This very God, the stainless one, is described in this *Bodhasāra*.
"I am ignorant, I do not know; who indeed am I?"—thus [one thinks]. Yet the state of being born from ignorance is the self, which is pure and stainless.

If this notion of the individual soul (*jīva*) that the Brahman is the object of meditation were [the truth], then the Self would indeed be a state consisting of delusion; yet the Self is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.3)
"I am bound by the three qualities; I wander in saṃsāra"—such are the primal states (prākṛta-bhāva); the Self, however, is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.4)

The fourfold set consisting of the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta) are states born of the internal organ; the Self (ātman), however, is pure and untainted.
That which is first conceptualized and, having been conceptualized, is then discriminated—these are states born of the mind; the self, however, is pure and stainless.
That which is determined as "this is thus" or "this is not thus" is indeed the nature consisting of consciousness; it is the self, pure and stainless.
States such as being a knower, an agent, an enjoyer, a victim, or a slayer arise from the ego; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
Memory is the recollection of what was previously experienced, and recognition is of a similar nature;
these states of being arise from the mind, while the self is pure and stainless.

The states that arise from the distinctions between the stages of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—namely, the Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—are [merely appearances]; the Self is pure and untainted. (NBs 17.10)
Sleep, laziness, negligence, delusion, and despondency—these states arise from *tamas*; the self, however, is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.11)
Tranquility, solitude, gentleness, illumination, and clarity—these states consist of *sattva*; the self (*ātman*), however, is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.12)
Greed, fickleness of the senses, and the undertaking of actions—these states arise from *rajas*;
the self, however, is pure and stainless.
Injunction and prohibition, dharma and adharma, the auspicious and the inauspicious,
and all states conditioned by agency— the self is pure and stainless.
The act, the effect, and the instrument—therein are the various kinds of activities;
these states follow upon agency, whereas the Self is pure and stainless.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these states arise from the five elements; the self, however, is pure and stainless.
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth as the fifth—entities are composed of these five elements; the self is pure and stainless.
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the sense of smell as the fifth—these states consist of the organs of cognition; the Self is pure and stainless.
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and likewise the generative organ as the fifth—these are the states consisting of the organs of action; the Self is pure and stainless.
Sound consists of the distinctions of phonemes, such as the struck and the unstruck;
these entities, composed of various sounds, are the self, which is pure and stainless.
The notes Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Dhaivata—these states consist of the differentiation of sounds; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
Entities consist of various types of tactile sensations—such as cold, heat, softness, hardness, sharpness, and roughness; the self, however, is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.22)
Red, yellow, white, black, green, and even variegated—these entities consist of various forms of color, whereas the self is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.23)
Pungent, astringent, sweet, salty, sour, and bitter—these states consist of the various tastes; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
Various states consisting of different kinds of fragrance—such as perfumes, scents, sweet odors, and foul odors—the self is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.25)
Beings such as those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from sprouting consist of various types of living creatures; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
The gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, and so forth—these phenomena consist of the various classes of living beings; the self, however, is pure and stainless.
The dispositions arising from one's chosen deity—whether Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Sāvitra, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or others—the self is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.28)
The states arising from lineage and ancestral clans—such as Vāsiṣṭha, Gārgya, Śāṇḍilya, Bhārgava, Āṅgirasa, and so forth—the self is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.29)
The states arising from learning and conduct—such as those of the reciters of the Purāṇas, the grammarians, the astrologers, and the physicians—the self is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.30)

The easterners, northerners, westerners, and others, as well as the southerners and other such [divisions], are states arising from the distinctions of sacrificial rites; the Self, however, is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.31)
The painter, the scribe, the carpenter, the speaker, the reader, and others—these states arise from the differentiation of actions; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
The qualities arising from the beauty of the body— such as being golden-hued, large-eyed, and possessing the well-knit physique of a lion— the self is pure and stainless.
Those states born from physical deformity— such as being mute, blind, lame, deaf, one-eyed, or having webbed fingers— the self is pure and stainless.
The netherworld, the earth, heaven, the Mahar-loka, the Janas, and so forth—these are the various states arising from the divisions of the worlds; yet the Self is pure and stainless.
Lions, tigers, boars, bears, deer, monkeys, and so forth—these states arise from the various categories of animals; the self, however, is pure and stainless.
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and other such states arise from the differentiation of the constituent elements; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these five are born from the divisions of prāṇa; the self, however, is pure and stainless.
The serpent, the tortoise, the lizard, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these states consist of the subordinate vital breath; the Self is pure and stainless.
Fever, epilepsy, leprosy, and conditions such as wind, bile, and phlegm—all these states arise from the imbalance of the bodily constituents; the self, however, is pure and untainted.
Piṅgalā, iḍā, suṣumṇā, gāndhārī, hastikā, and so forth—these are states arising from the differentiation of the channels; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.

The states arising from the differentiation of the subtle body (*liṅga*), which consist of departing, going, and returning, and which bestow heaven or hell—the Self (*ātman*) is pure and stainless. (NBs 17.42)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth—these states arise from the distinctions of caste; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—these states arise from the stages of life (āśrama); yet the Self is pure and stainless.
The Kāpālikas, the Kṣapaṇakas, those who act according to their own whims, and the Digambaras—all these states originate from heresy; the Self, however, is pure and stainless.
Possessiveness is approved by the deluded, but not by those established in equanimity; even that state of "I-ness" is a mere appearance, for the Self is pure and stainless.
O wise one, both "I-ness" and "mine-ness" are like a mother and her son;
yet these two are mutual slayers, so do not touch even one of them.
When that state has arisen, all phenomena dissolve within it;

O wise one, you are that very state in which emptiness and non-emptiness are equal and have reached a state of equanimity; you are the pure Self, free from all taint.
Through the investigation of the fifty verses concerning the stainless God,
one shall go to the state of the stainless God.
The eightfold Yamunā is radiant, sweet, cool, and purifying; she is like the Yamunā river in her brilliance.
For that darkness which was seen by me after having analyzed [the object] is indeed an error.
As for what you say—that the Goddess of Consciousness is formless and yet radiant—behold my stainless heart, purified by her. (NBs 18.2)
As for what you say—that the Goddess of Consciousness is flavorless—how is it that Śaṅkara and other connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor constantly savor her? NBs 18.3.
As for what you say—that the Goddess of Consciousness is touchless and cool—behold: by her grace, the threefold suffering has departed from me.
As for what you say— that the Goddess of Consciousness is devoid of qualities and purifying—
look at those such as Kaca, Datta, Śuka, and others, who were purified by her.
Then the disciple asks:
"O Teacher, do you characterize by means of characteristics that are themselves characterized?
O Lord, characterize by means of characteristics so that that which is to be characterized may be characterized."
To this, the following reply is given:
In this case, as with the definition and the definiendum, here the definiendum is not the definition;
this definiendum is distinct from the definition, yet the definition itself is the definition here.
Just as a dark cloud appears in the form of an illusion within the pure and deep sky,
so too does ignorance appear in the form of an illusion within the pure and deep Brahman.
Is this collection of six stones perhaps fashioned from the moonlight of infinite millions of moons?
I beheld a cow made of stone, whose very form was one of joy.
It does not run, it does not strike, it neither eats nor drinks;
naturally pure, this [consciousness] remains possessed of joy and nourishment.
Within the lines of her body hair, millions of universes are scattered;
that boundless cow is composed of Kāśmīra stone.
They come, they go, they run, they dance, and they laugh;
these are reflections in the form of living beings, while she herself remains as she is.
Though sapless, she is as sweet as nectar; though devoid of qualities, she is dear to the virtuous;
though formless, she is exceedingly beautiful—she has been seen by me, but not heard.
With the tongue of the knowledge of Brahman, drink from this cow that constantly flows with nectar;
having become a stone-calf, drink from the stone-cow.
The fivefold sleep is that sleep in which the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep do not exist.
They possess the nature of the three states because they are free from all dualities.
Because it transcends all qualities, not even a trace of darkness exists there;
and because its nature is self-luminous, there is indeed no lack of illumination either.
For the attainment of which ascetics perform great austerities,
and the wise investigate the statements of the Vedānta.
The fruit here is the enjoyment of happiness; it is that very [enjoyment] which consists of the nature of bliss.
Because its essence is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it does not consist of a mere waste of time.
This innate [state] is easily attained by those of pure awakening, but difficult for those whose nature is attached to sense objects;
it is the sleep of Mādhava and others, and it yields great fruit.
The group of nine experiences has been described by my gurus, who are masters of the realization of their own bliss; my true nature is indeed the very density of that realization of one's own bliss.
By some particular aspect consisting of the density of my own bliss and awareness, I have experienced nothing but the density of my own bliss and awareness.

For those yogins who possess faith and devotion, who are distinguished by their learning and disciplined in training, who have abandoned the perception of reality in unreal objects, and for whom renunciation has reached its deepest intensity— when the mind, becoming wondrously transformed, vibrates incessantly with the manifestation of truth as truth, Hari, whose nature is non-conceptual supreme bliss, manifests spontaneously.

Withdraw craving; having withdrawn the collection of the senses, withdraw all activities; O mind, withdraw and withdraw any other mental focus, and even by consuming [them], become subtle. Enter within into the abode of the Self; once that state is slightly attained, your being, capable of shattering the door-panel of all ignorance, will abide firm.

"Why do you ask me with such a respectful mind, O holy one, about the stages of meditative absorption? Indeed, the darkness of delusion has surely departed and a great light has arisen. Now that the lamp of awakening has dawned within me, dispelling the dense state of self-attachment, the multitudes of mental fluctuations fly away instantly like moths to perish. (NBs_21.4)
Whether it be solid or dissolved, clarified butter does not cease to be clarified butter, O virtuous one; and such is the wonder of consciousness—that the mind is indeed that very non-dual reality.

Therefore, this practice of the dissolution of the mind is the means to that reality; but now that reality has been directly realized, even the labor of sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra) has been completely abandoned by me.
Once the favor of the wise has arisen and innate bliss has arrived, the arduous effort of yoga is abandoned by practitioners with indifference;
yet, just as this dense sleep—though not even desired—is forcibly induced, so too does the profound sequence of meditative absorption (samādhi) esteemed by the Sage proceed. 21.6.
When the reality of the Upanishads has been ascertained by a slender intellect submerged in the ocean of the nectar of meditation,
and when all phenomena have then been observed with an impartial mind, an innate density of pure awareness naturally arises.
This knowledge is honey-sweet, because honey is seen everywhere;
for even in the sun-tree of one's own body, abundant honey is perceived.
"May I behold Viṣṇu"—such was my heart's desire;
now, by the grace of Viṣṇu, the entire world is permeated by Viṣṇu.
The "Tenfold Manifestation of the Wise":
that wherein the non-existence of entities is described, therein existence itself is proclaimed.
O dear one, listen to the ninefold manifestation that bestows the bliss of intrinsic nature.
This sage, having abandoned base desires and the like and gone far away,
may sometimes even see them, yet they do not reach him.
Views of duality certainly do not stand before one who knows that [reality];
once recognized as faulty for being faulty, how could they show their face?
"Recognized as 'illusion, illusion,' she who undergoes all forms of transformation has gone somewhere beyond return; the stainless Sage remains established. (NBs 22.4)
"The objects of the senses have surely been conquered and struck with slaps;
therefore they do not approach him, and for that reason he will kill us."
Having abandoned craving for trivial things, the sage has attained a state free from thorns;
with his soul satisfied by the elixir of its own essence, he flourishes day by day.
"Having abandoned me, her former beloved, she now delights in ignorance";
thus, as if ashamed, ignorance does not come before my face.

Indeed, the fault of laziness would surely carry away even Indra’s prosperity;
for the more a wise man becomes lazy, the more he increases in that state.

An unprecedented object appears therein; therefore, this dream is superior.
Yet, the external visible world does not appear there; therefore, it is not a dream at all. (NBs 23.3)
Due to the absence of all objective entities, that state of deep sleep is of the nature of bliss;
therein there is neither insentience nor darkness, nor even that which is called deep sleep.

Therefore, the Śruti declares the Truth to be beyond the reach of speech and mind;
it is exactly as experienced by the sages, of this there is no doubt.
This is the limit of sacred tradition; this is the limit of asceticism;
this is the limit of instruction; this is the limit of discernment.
Everything that is to be heard has been heard by you through the words of the Vedas as Brahman;
if it is to become Brahman, then let it indeed become Brahman.
The fivefold lamp of awakening does not require a supporting vessel, nor does it depend upon oil.
It does not depend upon a brush, nor does it bear even the slightest bit of soot.
It does not cause heat for anyone, nor is it shaken by the wind;
it does not undergo destruction, and it destroys all darkness.
All entities appear as having a single form through its radiance;
in its presence, even a shadow—which is of the nature of illusion—would not appear. (NBs 24.3)
That which is not an object of the eyes and is devoid of the form of matter, which cannot be manifested even by the mind, yet is the illuminator of the form of matter; // NBs_24.4 //
O dear one, at some time and in some place, for some reason or other,
this lamp of awakening arises within the palace of the hearts of the virtuous.
Empty the jar of the mind completely by means of the sixteen instructions, which are filled with reasonings and meditative applications.
Nothing whatsoever will come into being, dear one; there is no effort on the part of Brahmā in filling [the world].
Abandon anxiety, O one of great intelligence; resort to the bliss of being free from anxiety.
Tell me, who else but you would renounce this very anxiety that you yourself have acquired?
You must contemplate that object which is the medicine for the disease of anxiety;
or else, my dear, simply abandon the very disease called anxiety.
When nurtured, anxiety increases; when abandoned, it quickly perishes.
Even by such a malady, those of poor intellect have met their death.
Harsh, quarrelsome, a malevolent spell, barren, and eternally inauspicious—let this fierce craving be abandoned; let the beautiful Lady of Liberation be enjoyed.
When you are called "wise" by people, you attain supreme happiness;
therefore, become truly wise through your mind, actions, and speech.
Indeed, you are eternally of a radiant nature by virtue of being consciousness;
this world is merely a certain manifestation of you, whose very form is manifestation.
When it is known that "I, the luminous one, am mere light," and error has departed,
where is the second, where is saṃsāra, where is māyā, and what indeed is produced by it?
