A woman depicted on a variegated canvas, endowed with a wealth of diverse beauty, is seen only so long as the beautiful woman herself does not arrive. (NBs 43.44)
"Do not grieve over the wish-fulfilling gem fallen from your hand," my teacher said to me;
"in just a few days, it will surely be found again."
I harbor doubt as long as I have not beheld the face of Mukunda;
meanwhile, my mind is consoled by the Supreme Deity.
It has truly been said that Janārdana possesses the beauty of ten million Kandarpas;
at his manifestation, all those headed by Kandarpa fled.
While tears were shed by Rādhā, who was separated from him yet filled with hope for reunion,
Hari— previously hidden there by his illusory power (māyā)— became manifest.
Some wander about for the sake of fragrance, while others desire the honey; but those bees intoxicated by honey neither wander nor desire it.
A wood-carrier obtains wealth with great hardship during the evening;
a gem-examiner, seated comfortably, acquires abundant wealth.
A dancer may or may not obtain wealth through the graceful movements of her limbs;
however, a woman of noble family brings her husband under her control with a mere sidelong glance.
This radiance of your intellect tells me that liberation is near;
indeed, a lamp shines most intensely at the very moment of its extinction.
Some dig the earth, while others sell it;
some grind the gem, yet it is the fortunate one who enjoys its fruit.
Some are satisfied with buttermilk, while others are satisfied with curd or milk;
but those who know reality are not satisfied at all without butter and ghee.
A longing for sleep arose in me, thinking, "I shall sleep anywhere at all," yet I have obtained a vast, soft, and pure bed of Brahman.
The visible world, when rubbed away by awakening, attains the nature of pure consciousness;
wherever I look, it is my own form that is seen there.
When even a single person has been swallowed, people praise the python;
why do they not praise me, by whom tens of millions of world-systems have been swallowed?
One should not harbor malice toward me, even though I speak much;
I simply declare, "I am Brahman," for the Śruti does not hold malice toward me.
Samādhi is my lion-throne, the Vedānta texts are my panegyrists;
the enemy named Delusion has been slain, and my kingdom is free from thorns.
I have seen that which is called the sky of consciousness, a vast expanse; compared to which, this inert sky of matter is empty and exceedingly small.
Food is dear to one afflicted by hunger, wealth is dear to the wretched, water is beloved by the thirsty; likewise, consciousness is my favorite.
Just as copper, through contact with an elixir, has attained a state that is no longer copper,
so too has our egoism attained a state of non-egoism.
Previously, the ego was the cause of my suffering;
today that enemy is seen dead, becoming the cause of supreme bliss.
Just as a handsome young man who enjoys pleasures shines in the midst of those desiring enjoyment,
so does the knower of the ultimate truth shine in the midst of those seeking liberation.
Even while engaged in household duties, like a woman who has already experienced sensual pleasures,
the knower of yoga truly delights the mind with the mind alone.
Seeing the Sage filled with joy, the villager said to him repeatedly:
"Show me also that treasure which you have obtained."
O dear one, tell me: who has not been deceived by these deceptive sense-objects?
Surely even these tigers among men, the great teachers, have been deceived by them.
Let ignorant people pour thousands of jars of water upon his head;
the knower of the Self should maintain only silence, like the *śivaliṅga*.
But those teachers who possess reflection yet are detached are the best of teachers;
indeed, those who are detached even from reflection are the teachers of teachers.

Even a fool who merely desires to know gives up sense-objects that are like dust; for one who possesses such knowledge, what could possibly be difficult regarding the abandonment of attachment and aversion?
Even for those who have attained awakening, talk concerning the cycle of existence may arise,
just as talk about dreams persists for people even when they have reached the waking state.
When the object of perception is forgotten through delusion, deep sleep is experienced;
when the object of perception is forgotten through awakening, the fourth state remains.
If the visible world were non-existent, there would be only darkness; if the sun were non-existent, there would be no worldly activity. Thus it is said.
"If the sun did not exist, the world would not exist; indeed, it would then be mere darkness.
Such is the worldly condition, my son; now hear the way of ultimate reality.
For the sun is eternal for us; its destruction does not exist.
Even when everything has become darkness, it remains the witness of darkness—everlasting and imperishable.
For the sage who possesses meditative absorption, the sun exists but the world does not;
for this reason, O virtuous one, that light was indeed singular at that time.
For one who observes worldly conventions, the sun exists and the world exists;
for one who does not, the sun does not exist and the world does not exist—then indeed, there is only darkness.
O son, when that which is to be illuminated has vanished, what could illumination illuminate?
Even upon the destruction of the object to be illuminated, the nature of illumination remains unimpaired.
Whether it comes or goes, the light of the sun is manifested by its own causes;
for me, who am self-luminous, nothing whatsoever comes or goes.
O Great Sage, ask the mind about the greatness of the mind: is it bound or is it liberated?
If one should say that he is bound, then he is undoubtedly bound.
One might say, "You are partially liberated," or "You are partially liberated from delusion.
If one were to say, "You are liberated," then indeed you would be liberated from delusion.
Bound by a bound mind, one is bound; liberated by a liberated consciousness, one is liberated.
That this [self] is neither bound nor liberated—this is the definitive conclusion of Vedānta.
Whatever greatnesses manifest wherever they may be in the three worlds, all of them are attributes of the mind; for the mind is the locus of greatness.
Aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, and likewise garimā;
prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the qualities of the mind.
The mind is the bow, the mind is the string, and the mind alone is the archer;
the mind is the target, the mind is the piercing, and the mind pierced leads to liberation.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings.
What more need be said than this? For that [mind] does not abide in non-duality.

And he who, having severed with the sharp axe of awakening the internal organ— the sacrificial animal— endowed with the four feet of mind, ego, intellect, and the mental faculty, performs the slaughter of that beast for the fierce goddess; [he attains liberation].
Having attained supreme grace through the worship of the lotus feet of the fierce Ciccandī, it is no wonder that all supernatural powers (siddhis) roll eagerly at her feet.
The Eighteenth Chapter on Liberation while Living:
Having liberated the self from its bondage to volitional constructs by means of the self through the dissolution of those very constructs;
Satisfied with the self by means of the self, Hari himself delights in his own self.
Liberation is one's very own true nature, while worldly existence is pure ignorance;
O son, the state of one liberated while living is a most wondrous course.
Birth was assumed by the eternally liberated Self through sport for the sake of attaining the bliss of liberation while living, and not out of a desire for worldly existence.
If this deceptive drama called ignorance did not exist, how could the Self of the universe obtain the great festival of liberation while living? (NBs 46.4)
Non-duality does not exist for one with a body, nor does duality exist for one without a body;
this great festival of both duality and non-duality belongs neither to the one liberated while living nor to anyone else.
In one with a body there is no bodilessness; in one without a body there is no state of having a body.
Both the state of having a body and the state of being bodiless prevail in one who is liberated while living.
If the state of being disembodied could not belong to one who possesses a body, then tell me:
how was the state of being disembodied predicated of Janaka while he still possessed a body?
If being embodied were not possible for one who is disembodied, then tell me:
how was Janaka, who was disembodied, said to be embodied?
Liberation is established in the scriptures, and liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is well-ascertained;
without attaining the state of being liberated while living, there is no liberation of the disembodied self (*videhavimuktatā*).

Without knowledge there is no liberation; one who has died cannot become possessed of knowledge. The attainment of knowledge while living occurs; that is the unimpaired state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
If you ask, "What is the use of that happiness of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) which lasts for only a very short time? listen:
how is it that Sanaka and the others shine forth in the world of Brahmā?
Therefore, this is a certain divine play (līlā) of the Lord, taking the form of the Lord himself;
it is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which initiates the tradition of great liberation.
That state in which sages such as Nārada and others sport incessantly,
and which is experienced only by the wise— that is the inviolable liberation while living.
But those who, having abandoned the monastery that causes the distraction of the mind,
remain established in the ultimate state of nirvāṇa— they alone are the true ascetics, such as Sanaka and the others.
Those who, though consisting of inner awakening, appear as if intent on worldly activity while remaining established in their own steadfastness— they alone are Janaka and others like him.
Whether they live in a house or in the forest, those for whom steadfastness does not exist are neither among the likes of Sanaka and others, nor are they among the likes of Janaka and others.
For the wise possess inner substance and bestow nectar with few words;
indeed, the clouds of the rainy season thunder only very softly.
This Jīvanmukticaturdaśī should indeed always be studied and always meditated upon for the sake of attaining the state of liberation while living. (NBs 46.18)
The roar of the elephant of the wise resounds there; families of birds come there, sport, dwell, and fly away with great speed.
All things—whether equal, unequal, or diverse—are likewise in me; I alone am eternal, like the summit of the abode of the gods.
Emerging and submerging within that which consists of the world, those waves—high and low, beyond counting—arise by the turn of fate;
yet, having reached my final rest in my own greatness, which is established in immovability, I remain like the ocean, boundless and by my own nature.
Let the forest-dwellers such as Janmādi roam at will, and let the elephants of mental activity rub against my temples;
whether in this age, in a future age, or in any other age, I shall remain as immovable as the king of mountains.

Having properly placed my foot upon the summit of the Vindhya mountain, whose mass of delusion had been cast down, and having departed toward my desired direction, I have returned; I am Agastya, and I do not wander about according to my own whims.
"Today I saw someone whose facial radiance was fading, fallen to the earth from the third step;
therefore, a thought arose in me who knows both the higher and the lower: alas, heaven has an even more bitter ripening than hell!"
It is indeed better for one who has not ascended at all to remain in their natural state than to fall from having ascended to a lofty position due to ignoble conduct;
for alas, in that case, one's limbs are not shattered, nor is there distress in the mind, nor even the pain of ridicule.
If, having entered the channel, one lives in constant fear and devours [the breath] at the end, what is that long life?
But if, free from the nature of the body and abiding in the state of the Supreme Self, one conquers death, that indeed is long life.
The glances of the lords of sages have been observed, and many paths of great accomplishment have been beheld;
yet even today, having cast that state of impurity far away, why is success not achieved, if indeed it is eternally accomplished?
Having stretched out my limbs, I have indeed fallen into the nature of consciousness; having become drowsy, my activity has utterly ceased.
Like a rock on the Vindhya mountains extending for hundreds of yojanas, I neither diminish nor do I grow, remaining full.

My father, the king of all the world and the cause of steadfastness, intelligence, and strength, shines forth; my youth is fresh; and this beautiful woman of noble form has been wedded to me with great wisdom. Therefore, what greater happiness is there? Is there anyone more fortunate than I?
Possessing infinite contentment through contemplation on the state of the flavor of equanimity, having internally severed the thread of craving for even a moment’s fragment of pleasure,
and seated upon the lion-throne of the King of Vidyās— the treasure-trove of our own innate bliss— we spend our time here, supported by this body.
How many living beings—these kings of gods and others—do not wander through the cycle of existence with their hopes shattered by falling at the feet [of others]?
Having taken refuge at the feet of the Guru, we have become the boat of Brahman-knowledge and have reached the further shore; we are most truly blessed. (NBs 47.12)
The sky, though never stained by those who move through it, is eternally tasteless; the ocean of milk, despite being full of flavor, attains great increase only to release it again;
the Golden Mountain is the father of joys, yet he is not the refuge of joys, being tasteless, never diminishing, and never devoid of delight—there is nothing that equals me.
Though it appears multicolored at dawn and dusk, that sky is not the locus of various colors; no streak of water has ever been seen there.
Having plunged into it with wisdom, oh, I have beheld the stainless sky! The notion "blue, blue" is merely the fame of the sky; the blueness of the sky is false.

When a person of refined intellect formed the notion of silver regarding silver, while a person of poor intellect likewise did so regarding colored glass, both remained established in their own convictions through their respective cognitions, steadfast in their own certainty.
Yet, when the process of buying, selling, and expenditure occurred, the poverty of one alone was dispelled; thus, a clear distinction between the two became manifest.
Surely this is the nature of the ocean to flow downward; yet if the river were overturned by a wind from the Vindhya forest blowing in from somewhere, would the ocean not remain?
Or has it been moved from its place? On the contrary, even such a thing serves to proclaim the greatness of the sea.

The milk, having resorted to the state of being water, has now assumed the forms of curd and sourness—both trivial—and has thereby lost all its glory. But for gold, which assumes in turn the states of being a neck-ornament, an armlet, or even smallness and largeness, there is no loss of its own inherent nature.
Indeed, indeed, they are not clever who have not realized the pure Buddha; indeed, indeed, they are not skillful who have not gone to the further shore;
indeed, indeed, they are not of noble lineage who have not discerned reality; indeed, indeed, they are not sages by whom the pursuit of greed has been maintained.
O ego, you have no further task here; become dissolved in your own greatness, which is established in immovability.
O mind, come within to the supreme ocean of your own bliss; we are unable to endure these wicked tendencies of yours.
O son, mental disturbances never arise there; if they do arise here, reflect upon this and remain silent.
You too should move about slowly here; abandon delusion if you have the desire for that state of mine, the treasure-house of bliss.
The darkness is intense; this is the time known as midnight; moreover, the location is full of thieves and the wall is fragile.
Such being the case, if the householder remains vigilant and guards his own wealth, the thieves will indeed be frustrated.
Noble rulers who wield sharp weapons should engage in the hunt to subdue the wicked deer;
if the wicked deer is not slain but others are killed instead, tell me, what power does that king possess? For his effort is in vain.
When what is desired is lost and all things are perishable, one who has renounced enjoyments, developed the sense of "enough," and become free from passion,
spontaneously attains each successive stage, subtle by subtle, which practitioners finally achieve.
If they possess discursive thought within the heart, then their activity is not correct; following after [false] paths, they partake only in suffering.
Consider how those who are led by the blind, like the blind themselves, fall into a dark well even when gathered together in a crowd.
One said, "Recite for me"; another said, "Go to the distant forest"; another said, "Kindle the fire"; and yet another said, "Behold the sun.
To one desiring a good sacrifice, these were the words spoken by my elders: "You alone are that; for the attainment of a good sacrifice, these others do not see, even though their eyes are rolling."
Let the talk of those book-demons—who have cheeks as firm as a diamond or tongues a span long—remain for the sake of fame or for quarreling.
Ask me, O Śamatha, how meditation shines forth, what is retention, what is the true nature [of reality], by what natural flavor, and by what method the mind dissolves into the Supreme.
O Goddess Tongue, observe silence now; you have spoken enough. If your mind is established in the inner reality (*pratyag-vastu*), then why these idle prattlings?

O Crooked One, since your heart is fixed upon the beauty of the waves of the nectar-ocean that naturally subsides [of its own accord], you have for the most part become harsh; therefore, you do not please me.

When the Supreme Brahman is perceived, the entire world is indeed the Nandana grove; all trees are wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees; the waters of the Gaṅgā are all bodies of water; all actions are meritorious; both Prakrit and Sanskrit are the words of the Vedas; the earth is Vārāṇasī; and every state of existence is the path to liberation. (NBs 47.28)

In that [Self] this entire manifold world is woven across and lengthwise, wherein it exists, and wherein it arises and dissolves again like waves in water; that mind dissolves daily into Me, and from Me alone it is born. Therefore, O knowers of dissolution, tell me: where then do I myself dissolve? 47.29.
The young girl, restrained by her mother-in-law, casts her long gaze from the threshold toward the face of the youth adorned with the beauty of youth;
yet, though he stands thus, her mental state does not waver from him whose brow she gazes upon—a man who is the very abode of the Fortune of Liberation.

For that ocean of consciousness which is without end and possesses such vast profundity that countless clay-molds of universes sink within it yet do not shine forth—what can I say of its delicious flavor and its nature, so great? To whom is it an object, and who could possibly be its speaker? (NBs 47.31)

I shall declare before the Lord of Ramā, or else before the Lord of Gaurī, or even before the Lord who consists of the Word-Brahman— before anyone at all— that realization which, being supremely luminous and inclined toward Prahlāda, has blossomed without crookedness from consciousness within a tranquil mind full of wonder.

When the Sage beheld his own stainless nature—dissolved by cravings, risen through forbearances, opened by wisdoms, set by delusions, shaken by errors, and driven far away by dualities; yet shimmering with insights, sporting with joys, and closed in upon itself by doubts—he shone forth. (47.33)

"What was the difference between the former name and this one that did not appear before? Or what cause has now arisen by which this is perceived?"—with minds thus filled with wonder, the wise remain dissolved in the Supreme Brahman, the abode of the Lord of Sages, within that Forest of Bliss thick with the sleep of higher knowledge.
When pure awakening flashes forth on all sides, the stains of latent impressions are washed away; the mind is stilled, detachment has arisen, and the bonds of karma are shattered.

Duality is broken, bliss is attained, and conceptualization is cast far away. When reality is seen as clearly as a jujube fruit in the palm of one's hand, there remains no further duty to be performed.
By the mere name of Narahari, that wicked Hiraṇyakaśipu— though exceedingly powerful— is utterly torn asunder.
Therefore, assuming the form of the Man-Lion, you must tear apart Hiraṇyakaśipu, who deludes the mind.
Even after attaining the sovereignty of Indra, his own enemy—consisting of greed and craving—did not reach satisfaction;
thinking, "Now my welfare lies in its very destruction," Nṛhari, whose self is wisdom, brought about its destruction.
It is said that the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu was as hard as adamant, such that all weapons were blunted against it;
yet that very chest was torn open by your claws, O Nṛhari—this power of your claws is truly marvelous!
The inner vision is the heart; situated at the tip of the heart, the radiant Nṛhari led that darkness to its end.
All suffering reached a state of destruction, and Prahlāda alone attained supreme greatness.
He who could not be slain from within nor yet from without, neither by day nor by night, neither by the wet nor by the dry-bodied;
he who was not to be struck down by man nor by beast—such an enemy Narahari slew in a most wondrous manner.

Narahari is eternally present everywhere—in both the stationary and the moving—yet by divine providence, he manifested once more even within a mere lump of stone; that Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was the very foundation of such a vast cosmic expansion, was brought to non-existence—all this was indeed performed out of a desire for the joy of his own people.
If one sings the six-fold Vāra mantra in the heart after having conquered the six enemies that are the senses,
this six-fold Nara-hari mantra wards off the six-fold group of mental afflictions.
The Hundred Verses on the Raving of a Madman:
Tasting the nectar of pure awareness, I prattle like one who is intoxicated.
May the intellects of the virtuous purify the hidden meaning of that rambling discourse.
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy—
listen now to the detailed explanation of how these very things become the means for crossing over saṃsāra.
Those who are greedy for the beauty of the pleasure of union with Viśrāntisundarī,
who are adept in exclusive dalliance, and who are full of longing, go to liberation.
That very anger, by whose power the Yogin Narahari himself tore open the chest of the Daitya Mōha, is the means for liberation.
He whose face is incapable of being looked upon because it is distorted by a frown—
the mental states such as desire and greed— is the hater who is dear to Keśava.
O dear one, for those who are perfectly serene regarding the eternal and frowning toward the impermanent,
liberation stands in the palm of their hand, even though they possess passion and hatred.
By that greed with which the Sage purchases the wish-fulfilling jewel of knowledge by giving away the glass trinket of the mind,
that very greed becomes the means to liberation.
That delusion by which one forgets through love for the consciousness the social classes, stages of life, conduct, body, enjoyments, wealth, and so forth— that very delusion is the supreme state.
"There is nothing else superior to me; I alone am the Great Lord (Maheśvara);
I alone am the highest"—this kind of pride is considered the bestower of liberation.
But he who, by the power of the excellence of his knowledge, does not tolerate the excellence of what is seen—
that one is superior to a sage free from envy for a hundred years.
The virtues of those who possess patience are bound to the big toe of the left foot of him who cannot endure even for a moment the outward flickering [of the senses].
Desire and the like are great rogues by whom the three worlds have been robbed;
he who outwits them through skillful means is himself a rogue, beloved of Dhūrjaṭi.
He who indulges in greed and the other inner roots, while cutting them off externally, is merely another form of hypocrisy; he attains liberation within.
He who constantly whispers into the ear of everyone, even those possessed of virtuous qualities, the very faults of their inner selves— that slanderer is one who partakes in liberation.
I have seen that crest-jewel of sages who, though he always harbored slander of others within his heart, has nonetheless attained the supreme state.
For those whose minds are certain that "this entire world is indeed false," that world is difficult to attain for speakers of falsehood; it belongs to the speaker of truth.
"He who says, 'I do nothing at all,' while being devoid of right conduct—
the practitioners do not go to the same destination as that non-practitioner."
Having abandoned even those former friends such as discernment and the rest,
he who has gone beyond them is liberated as one who has transcended attachment to friends.
He by whose illusion the universe, consisting of the five elements, was created—
he indeed was seen by me as the wielder of illusion, the vessel of liberation.
He who creates the universe by his own will alone and destroys it by his own will alone— he,
though ungrateful, is more worthy of worship than even the grateful man, for he attains liberation.
It is a marvel that he who conceives of the individual soul as the Lord attains,
by virtue of that very conceit, a state that is otherwise difficult to reach for those devoid of egoism.
Perceiving faults even in virtues, reviling the entire world,
and intent on self-praise, they go eternally to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Even though he has realized the pure Self, like a person in the world of conventional usage,
the beloved of Śambhu acts while saying "I do not act," practicing hypocrisy.
With the sharp sword of awakening, he slays the killer— the sin accumulated over hundreds of previous births— of those possessed of delusion, egoism, and evil intellect.
"‘I am Hari, I am Brahmā, I am Śiva’—those who kill with such confidence are meritorious slayers of the trusting. (NBs 49.24)

Freed from injunctions and prohibitions, carefree and wandering according to his own will, he is one whom the ritualists would exclude from their assembly; yet, for us, he is the purifier of the assembly.
Those two who are censured—namely, one who has abandoned his duties and one who has exceeded his term—are indeed pure for us;
for he who has abandoned his duties and he who has exceeded his term are always purified by the sacrificial fire.
The sage who, having closed the door at his entrance, eats sweet food alone like a piece of broken *laḍḍuka* dessert, goes to the supreme goal.
He by whom the host of the organs of knowledge and action was restrained within its own abode,
brought into a single line, and destroyed— he is the purifier of our assembly.
Behold, for those who hate cyclic existence and endure the destruction of the self for the sake of destroying cyclic existence, liberation is described in the scriptures.
In the gambling match of awakening, he who has lost everything— namely, the notions of "I" and "mine"—
is declared in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti to be a partaker of liberation.
He in whom there is no compassion even for the deer-like beings with their feeble senses—
he alone is most dear to the Son of Devakī, the friend of the distressed.
But that king who, devoted to his own enjoyments, does not look after the city, is not tainted by sin; the Muṇḍaka Śruti is the authority for this.
For one who has slain the wealth of the mind with the noose of knowledge and dispassion—
whoever is such a master of the noose— for him Kāśī is at every step.
He who forcibly enjoys the company of an ascetic widow between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is pure, for he is one whose addiction to widows has been exhausted.
He by whom the dense forest of duality has been burnt by the forest fire of awakening indeed attains the most meritorious state; he is truly the one who provides the forest fire.
Even for those staying at home, he who gives a mouthful of grass to cows and does not practice nourishing himself is liberated from all sins.
All the flavors have been sold by him who, ignorant of dharma and adharma, has bound the wealth of awakening within his knot; blessed is that seller of flavors!
He who, as the inner controller (antaryāmin), brought about the confusion of castes,
is himself described as Śaṅkara, yet he is one who causes the confusion of castes.
He who, having thoroughly studied the Vedas and understood their meaning through his own reflection,
has caused them— along with the Vedāntas— to overflow [with realization], is a "bather of the Vedas" (vedaplāvī) and is liberated.
Everything offered to Śiva becomes the *nirmālya* of Śiva;
the pure-souled one who eats that *nirmālya* of Śiva partakes of it. (NBs 49.40)
One who has entered the life of celibacy may enjoy all the women of the city;
he is not stained by sin—wonderful indeed is the vision of the Vedānta!
Having tasted some of the remnants fallen from the mouths of yogins, avadhūtas, Śuka, and others, one who eats such remnants shall be liberated.
Brahmā knows only that very brāhmaṇa of pure mind by whom the cessation of [worldly] activity has been performed;
he is the blessed one who effects the cessation of activity.
But for that sage who, by chance, eats a brinjal, burnt food, kalañja, or the like, Hari is indeed not far away.
The Vāruṇī Brahma-vidyā was indeed taught by Varuṇa to Bhṛgu;
it is the supreme goal for those intoxicated by the tasting of the essence of that Vāruṇī.
Having abandoned the outward-turned state, that which is inward-turned is indeed the Vāruṇī;
for those devoted to its practice, the supreme state is not far off.
Having beheld a beautiful woman who is like a flash of lightning, those whose mind— the lord of the senses— is deranged by the senses, yet claim to be liberated, are not masters of their senses.

Having ascended the stage of yoga into the profound ocean of Brahman, one subsequently falls back and becomes despondent; such a person is "one who has fallen after ascending" (ārūḍhapatita), yet remains pure.
I have performed my bath in the river Karmanāśā, where consciousness, ignorance, and karma are destroyed;
by touching the waters of Karmanāśā, the bondage of karma is dissolved.
In Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Saurāṣṭra, and Magadha,
I am everywhere fully present, yet again, devoid of all mental impressions.
"He who, having abandoned his own home, takes delight in the house of another—that householder shall attain the supreme goal; such is the opinion of the wise. (NBs 49.51)
He who, out of greed for his own pleasure, has squandered his merit—he alone is truly meritorious; for the rest, even while performing good deeds, are in fact doers of evil.
Those for whom ignorance itself is knowledge, non-discrimination is discrimination, and identity with all things is absolute liberation— they are the most excellent of the perfected ones.
Śaṅkara has said that liberation belongs to those who, through focused attention, destroy that mind which produces errors. (NBs 49.54)
Through the form of reciting the Vedānta, my own duties were proclaimed by me;
and by that very proclamation of my own duties, the state of union (sāyujya) was attained.
If a Brahmin who has two wives should abandon his first wife, who is devoted to her husband,
out of greed for the qualities of the other, he goes to the supreme destination.
The explanation of this is as follows: "Engagement and withdrawal are the two wives ordained by the Veda;
the first consists of devotion to ritual action, while the other consists of devotion to Brahman. (NBs 49.57)
*Karkaśā* and *Rasikā* are their other names respectively;
*Karkaśā* abides in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), while *Rasikā* is a proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādinī*).
Although there are two types of devoted wives, the *rasikā* and the *karkaśā*,
the *rasikā* enjoys her own husband, while the *karkaśā* is a partaker of suffering.
But one devoted to action is like a maidservant, always engaged in household chores;
whereas one devoted to knowledge is a great queen seated upon the lion-throne of royalty.
For the sake of her husband, let her perform her household duties by day and by night;
how can she who possesses such good fortune sleep without embracing her husband?
One who speaks harshly of her duties does not know the aesthetic flavor (rasa) or the poetic style (rīti);
yet a woman devoted to her husband by nature praises her husband alone.

But she who is devoted to gnosis, being a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor through the characteristics of various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), delights her husband and sports while embracing him alone. (NBs 49.63)
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, or at a meal, she was always with him;
for a moment the master did not remain without her, being so eager for her pleasure.
But he who, through his discernment, knows the great difference between these two—how could he take pleasure in that which is deluded? What joy, indeed, is there in it?
But whoever is a great fool, a vulgar person possessing the nature of a beast,
delights in the harsh and does not find the true aesthetic flavor.
In her he finds suffering and quarrels with her every day;
yet he continues to pursue her alone—such is his misfortune.
In this regard, concerning the meaning of the scripture on having two wives, this rule is established:
having abandoned a woman who has turned away from worldly activity, one who pursues her would go to hell.
Having abandoned the woman that is worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*), one who has turned away from it attains liberation (*mokṣa*).
Although this meaning of the scripture is difficult to grasp, it is authoritative by virtue of the words of Vyāsa.
Thus concludes the exposition of the scriptures concerning engagement and withdrawal.
Now, another point as well:
if the statement made by Vyāsa—that Viṣṇu alone is the Great Being—should be accepted;
When those great elements have ceased to move, the supreme state is not far off.
This mantra of the ḍākinīs is "I am Brahman" (brahmāsmi), consisting of these syllables; by the mere power of its meditation, one immediately attains that very nature.
Having attained the supreme state through the grace of the Guru and the scriptures, that excellent one declared: "This is mine alone; it has been obtained by me."
But for that which has not been attained in reality at all, even through cognitions practiced over hundreds of births— its attainment is the greatest of all.
That which perceives the greatness of the minute, the proximity of the distant,
and the nature of the other as one's own self— that indeed is valid cognition.
That which is seen is false; that which is not seen is true.
This indeed is the authoritative principle according to the Great Upaniṣads.
He whose entire diverse composition appears devoid of flavor is praised in the Śruti as one liberated while living, who is equal to one who is dead while yet alive.
Just as a lamp might shine by itself in an empty house,
the birth of that lamp, whose shining would otherwise be useless, is described as meaningful.
This lamp of awakening does not reveal even the slightest difference between itself and entities;
for us, this very lamp of non-awakening is the lamp of awakening.
I remain awake only during the night and sleep throughout the entire day;
nor do diseases such as old age, death, and the like afflict me.

The appearance of distinctions among superior, inferior, and middling cognitions is the fruit of those [cognitions]; for one who is devoid of them, Hari has proclaimed the state of being a supreme sage.
"O Pārtha, Janārdana said that he alone is truly endowed with wisdom, by whom both good and evil deeds have been abandoned through the intellect."
He for whom there is no concern for what has been done or left undone, and who has no dependence anywhere—
him Pārthasārathi calls "insignificant," yet he possesses pure liberation.
"He who knows neither dharma nor adharma, knows neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious, and knows neither pleasure nor pain—he is considered a man of knowledge by Hari. (NBs 49.83)
"It is everywhere described that liberation comes through contemplation alone;
however, in our own view, one should not contemplate anything at all within oneself."
The contemplation of all treatises is one view; my own view is another.
It is simply through the absence of any contemplation that reality itself manifests spontaneously.
When the reality is revealed by oneself, one becomes identical with it at that very moment.
Since not even a single quality exists in it, how indeed could there be two or three?
For Govinda sings of the qualities of that which is beyond the three qualities (niṣtraiguṇya).
He who has no qualification for any ritual action whatsoever is proclaimed by the Son of Nanda as the primary qualified person for absolute liberation.
To him who denies direct perception while seeing, hearing, touching, and smelling, and who says, "I do nothing at all," Keśava spoke thus to that noble one: NBs_49.88.
Mādhava has declared those to be virtuous who, even though they know the true path, do not teach it to the deluded, but instead praise the deluded path. (NBs 49.89)
The charioteer of Pārtha praised that very path of the yogis, by entering which one suffers a fall in a future birth.
For the restraint of spontaneous activity grants success to the practitioners of Haṭha-yoga;
however, for us practitioners of Jñāna-yoga, spontaneous activity itself is liberation.
Even having slain these worlds, he who does not kill and is not bound—
according to our view, his association is the means to peace.
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Regarding this unavoidable [process], my considered view is that there is no escape.
The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes for that person;
the state of one whose actions have thus been consumed cannot be attained by those devoted to ritual action.
But he who is a base man, even if he has departed from all desires, is truly one who seeks the purpose of man; so said the Supreme Person.
The Viṣṇugītā has been studied by me, and the definitive conclusion therein has emerged:
one who renounces all dharmas is liberated from all sins.
This discourse concerning the object that is non-attachment is indeed appropriate;
when meditated upon again and again, it bestows upon the virtuous the state of perfect non-attachment.
When this [author] engages in the investigation of improper domains through censurable paths such as sensual desire,
his *Śataka* becomes manifest as the ravings of a madman.
"O Father, do not disregard this because it is the ravings of a madman;
surely its true meaning is difficult to understand for those whose souls are attached to sense objects."
Thus has this "Madman's Raving" been proclaimed by me to you by name.
"Surely [he speaks thus] with a mind constantly fixed on one point and always one-pointed"—
this must be considered as the ravings of a madman by one of cultivated intellect.
For those of great intelligence who have become intoxicated by the state of Manonmanī, this outpouring is their treasure;
let it be established in the temple of the heart.
The *Śivapūjāśataka* is a work consisting of the worship of Śiva, capable of uprooting all karma.
The resolve for the worship of Śiva removes the suffering of all worldly desires.
The initiation into the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva, consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), is beneficial;
one who is proficient in the Word-Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman.
The three lines of *vibhūti*— representing faith, devotion, and dispassion—
should be worn on one’s limbs by the followers of Śambhu for the sake of attaining the qualification for worship.
One should wear Rudrākṣa beads and the Rudrābharaṇa mudrās;
"Becoming a god, one should worship the God"—this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
Now, the sequence of worship:
That which consists of clay is worshipped by the Śaivas as the *śivaliṅga*, in which the forms of Brahmā and others, as well as all moving and stationary beings, are imagined. (NBs 50.5)

In that regard, first is the taking up of the earth with the mantra "Salutation to Hara. That clay from which millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa) are said to arise as mere shards, that very clay should be taken by the wise with the words "Salutation to Hara. (NBs 50.6)
"Salutation to Maheśvara"—this is the union of the *liṅga*.
That which is described in the Vedānta as the mental state (*vṛtti*) of undivided form is indeed this "union of the *liṅga*" expressed as "salutation to Maheśvara. (NBs 50.7)
"Salutation to the wielder of the trident"— with these words, the installation is performed.
Having abandoned both lack of conviction and the cultivation of contrary notions,
the wise should install the wielder of the trident upon the pedestal consisting of the ultimate realization.
"Salutation to the wielder of the Pināka bow"—this is the invocation.
"Even for the omnipresent God, devotion is your invocation;
I invoke you with devotion"—thus is the wielder of the Pināka bow to be invoked.
Now, regarding meditation:

One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa—the primordial source of the universe, worshipped by all, the remover of all fears, five-faced and three-eyed—seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, wearing a tiger skin, radiant with jewel ornaments, adorned with the beautiful crescent moon, holding in his hands an axe, a deer, the gesture of granting boons (*vara*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and gracious in countenance. NBs_50.10 //
Now follows its commentary.
Therein is the commentary on the three words beginning with "dhyāyet" (one should meditate):
"Those who are eternally disenchanted with the impermanent and eternally firm in their vows regarding the permanent."
Those who discern between the eternal and the non-eternal constantly meditate upon Maheśa.
Now follows the explanation of the phrase "resembling a mountain of silver":
Śambhu is the mountain of silver, the supreme wealth of the devotees of Śambhu;
for those who are filled with that wealth, poverty does not exist.

Now, the explanation of the phrase "one who has the beautiful moon as his crest-ornament" (cārucandrāvataṃsa): The supreme, pure-souled, cool, lovely, subtle, and awakening digit [of the moon], which is difficult to attain, acts in a crooked manner; he whose crest is the moon bears that digit. (NBs 50.13)

Now, the explanation of the phrase "whose limbs are radiant with a jeweled ornament" (ratnākalpojjvalāṅga): Śaṅkara bestows certain jewels of awakening that consist precisely of the initiation of yoga; therefore, his limbs are radiant with a jeweled ornament.
Now follows the explanation of the hand holding the axe:
That sharp axe of awakening, by which the forest of delusion— once cut down— never again sprouts, resides in the hand of Rudra.

Now follows the exposition of the "Deer in Hand": That deer of the mind, which cannot be captured even by the steadfast and flees even when seized, was held in the hand by Śambhu with effortless ease.

Now follows the explanation of the state of having a boon-bestowing hand (*varahastatva*). Śaṅkara is the "Boon-giver" (*varada*) because he bestows that very boon upon those seekers of boons by whom he has been chosen as the most excellent one for the sake of a boon; it is by means of his hand that he grants the boon.
Now follows the explanation of the state of having fearlessness in hand: Even Brahmā fears death; death itself is the great terror.
Therefore, that which is deathlessness and fearlessness is in the hand of Mṛtyuñjaya.
Now, the explanation of the term "serene" (*prasanna*):
Having attained even a single accomplishment (*siddhi*), someone may become inwardly serene;
but Hara, when ever-serene, is the treasury of all accomplishments. (NBs 50.19)
Now follows the explanation of the term "seated upon a lotus" (*padmāsīna*):
Because Sadāśiva is ever seated within the lotus-hearts of the virtuous,
for that very reason he is described in the Vedas as "seated upon a lotus."
Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with "Then, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals": Humans praise the gods, and those gods praise the leaders of the gods;
the God of Gods, Mahādeva, is praised by the leaders of the gods.
Now follows the explanation of the verse beginning with "wearing a tiger-skin":
"By Śaṅkara, in the guise of a hunter, the tiger of delusion was struck down; behold the illustration of this in his [the hunter's] tiger-skin form upon his hips. (NBs 50.22)
Now follows the explanation of the phrase "the first of all, the one to be venerated by all":
He is the creator of all, whose form is the universe, the heart of all, and the protector of all;
he is the first of all, the one to be venerated by all, the Lord of all, and the husband of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Now follows the explanation of the term *nikhilabhayahara* ("the remover of all fear"):
"The Veda declares that fear arises from duality; indeed, fear comes from a second [entity].
Hara removes every fear of his devotees, for he is the bestower of liberation. (NBs 50.24)
Now follows the explanation of the term "five-faced" (*pañcavaktra*):
"Devotees meditate [upon Him] everywhere; He faces all of them, while He turns His face away from those who are averse. That is His state of being five-faced. (NBs 50.25)
Now follows the explanation of the term "Three-eyed" (Trinetra):
Ritual action and meditative worship are the two eyes; knowledge is the third eye.
He upon whose forehead that [third eye] shines is Śaṅkara, the Three-eyed One.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.
Now follows the investigation of the requisites;
therein, first is the investigation into the quality of resembling pure crystal.
In that which is stainless, all this indeed reflects;
like pure crystal, this Lord is free from passion.
Now, the consideration of the camphor-white radiance:
By the grace of which latent impression all evil impressions have vanished,
that very nature which is cool by its own essence— O Śivā, this is the camphor-white radiance.
Now, the consideration of the state of being sky-clad (Digambara):
For Hara himself, whose essential nature is unobscured consciousness, wanders freely through saṃsāra; therefore he is called Digambara.
Now follows the consideration of smearing oneself with ashes:
"The fire of knowledge indeed reduces all actions to ashes;
with that very ash, Dhūrjaṭi (Śiva) smears his body. (NBs 50.30)
Even for things that appear distinct, no difference exists in the ashes;
by virtue of their own inherent nature, the ashes belong to Bharga.
Now, the consideration of the state of having the moon as a crest-jewel:
All of his digits perish, yet that digit which has been offered with devotion to Śaṅkara does not perish at all; by that [digit], Hara becomes the Moon-crested One.
Now, the consideration of the matted locks:
This ancient banyan tree is Hara, the place of rest for the lords of sages;
the three known as Vedānta, Sāṅkhya, and Yoga are remembered as its matted locks.
Now, the consideration of Gaṅgādhara:
Hara is called Gaṅgādhara because the Gaṅgā, which originates from the world of Brahmā, is the Suṣumṇā, a cool liquid, and she shines upon his head.
Now, the consideration of the three-eyed nature:
He is the nourisher, the destroyer of darkness, and the burner of defects through his knowledge;
because he has the moon, the sun, and fire as his eyes, Śaṅkara is therefore "Three-eyed."

Now, the investigation into the state of having a blue throat (*nīlakaṇṭhatā*): The cause of the blue throat is the shadow of the various universes and skies swallowed in many ways within his throat, which resembles crystal. (NBs 50.36)
Because the space situated at the throat-region of the Lord of Pārvatī, whose body is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), is dark blue,
Hara is therefore called Nīlakaṇṭha.
Because the compassionate Śaṅkara held that poison-water, white as a cloud,
upon his neck, he is therefore as beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud upon his throat.
Resembling pure crystal, he stands upon Mount Mandara;
the hue of the sapphire mountain is the cause of the blue throat of the Blue-Throated One.
Rāma is his supreme devotee, and Śaṅkara is affectionate toward his devotees;
it was for the sake of becoming "Blue-throated" (Nīlakaṇṭha) that he wore the jewel of Rāma around his neck.
Now, an investigation into the state of being adorned with serpents:
Yogis who subsist on air and likewise dwell in mountain caves maintain their own true form; for that reason, Hara is adorned with serpent ornaments.
A certain Kuṇḍalinī power was brought under control by Śaṅkara;
through that Kuṇḍalinī, [all beings] became possessors of earrings (Kuṇḍalins), having attained the state of being ornaments for the body.
Ananta and Vāsuki have become the earrings of Śambhu;
because they are preeminent among them, the others as well are known by the designation "Kuṇḍalin."
Now follows the contemplation on the trident:
With his three swift prongs known as peace, dispassion, and awakening,
the Three-eyed One destroys the triple city of the three qualities by means of the trident.

Now follows the consideration of the hand-drum (ḍamaru). Under the guise of its rattling sound, this drum repeatedly proclaims "not this, not this" for the sake of the liberation of the followers of Śiva; for it is indeed the drum of Śambhu.

Now follows the consideration of the garland of severed heads: "Indeed, Śiva alone is capable of wearing the garland of heads consisting of the infinite and eternal cosmic eggs, because his own form is beginningless and endless. (NBs 50.46)
Now, the consideration of the bull-vehicle:
Śaṅkara mounts that [vehicle] upon which Brahmā and the others do not mount;
because it is the meditative absorption called Dharmamegha, he is therefore the "Bull-vehicled One."
Now, the investigation of Kailāsa:
Rudra shines in Kaivalya (absolute liberation), and his devotees likewise always shine there;
by virtue of that play of Kaivalya, Kailāsa is the abode of Śambhu.
Now, the consideration of Mount Mandara: That awakening named Mandara, by which this ocean of existence was churned for the sake of the jewel of liberation— that is the abode of Śaṅkara.
Now, the investigation of the cremation ground: In that cremation ground of cyclic existence where this Saṃhārabhairava himself eternally sports, Śiva is seen everywhere.
Now, the consideration of the *gaṇas*:
Śambhu is the ocean of bliss, and his power is said to be its fluid;
the *gaṇas* are like droplets from the ocean, those drops of bliss.
The Lord is distinct from the world by virtue of His essential nature, form, and characteristics;
that His attendants are likewise distinct from the world—what wonder is there in that?
Now, the investigation of the host of Yoginīs:
Whatever mental fluctuation belongs to yogis through the practice of yoga, that very thing has approached Śambhu; this indeed is the host of Yoginīs.
These companions of Śaṅkara— Yoginīs, Bhairavas, and so forth—
are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), yet they are called by the ignorant to be ghosts, spirits, and demons.
Now follows the consideration of Kālabhairava:
Time, who has rolled back the web of the world, is his doorkeeper;
that host which is the universe itself, yet fears Time, is Kālabhairava.
Now, the consideration of Daṇḍapāṇi:
By the very act of restraining the mind, one becomes a member of the Gaṇa of Daṇḍapāṇi;
for it is precisely such persons who attain the status of being a Gaṇa of the Lord.
Now follows the consideration of the Kṣetrapālas:
Śambhu himself is the Supreme Self, and the Kṣetrapālas are his portions;
surrounded by the Kṣetrapālas through the distinction of the relationship between the whole and its parts, Hara is encompassed.
Now, the consideration of the group of Nandis:
That consciousness whose form is seen shimmering above the Supreme Lord,
being of the nature of pure being, is celebrated as Nandikeśvara.
Now, the consideration of Bhṛṅgin:
He who, in the form of a bee-insect, was devoted [to Śiva] and attained similarity of form (sārūpya),
he indeed became the Gaṇa named Bhṛṅgin of Khaṇḍaparaśu.
Now, the investigation of Mahākāla:
The universe is devoured by Time; Time is devoured by Awakening.
This one, whose nature is Awakening, is the Time of Time—Mahākāla, the supreme Gaṇa.
Now, the investigation of Skanda:
He by whom the army of delusion was routed through the force of his own awakening—
that wise Mahāsena, the son of Śiva, is named Skanda.
Now follows the consideration of Gaṇeśa: Another son is the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvara), who destroys the mass of obstacles, is proficient in all branches of knowledge,
is visibly plump with bliss, and is the direct bestower of spiritual accomplishments.
Now, the consideration of Śivarātri:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled one keeps watch;
he who keeps watch on Śivarātri—Śiva is pleased with him. (NBs 50.63)
The five organs of action and the five organs of cognition,
along with the mind (manas), the ego (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (citta)— these three— and the intellect (buddhi) as the fourteenth.
This fourteenth day of Śivarātri has been proclaimed by the followers of Śambhu;
on that occasion, the wise man should restrain his conduct through fasting.
O son, this Śivarātri, performed by devotees of Śiva from of old, is exceedingly dear to Śiva and bestows union with Śiva.
For the Lord, midnight itself is midday and night itself is day;
that wherein nothing at all appears is the light of Śambhu.
Now follows the investigation of Śiva’s Tāṇḍava dance:
Know that the Śāmbhava Tāṇḱava, which is called the sport of bliss, is that by whose very absorption in bliss Nārada and the others are delighted. (NBs 50.68)
Now follows the consideration of [the Lord] as the Destroyer of Smara (Smarahara).
When Smara has been destroyed, these six—Smara and the others—are indeed destroyed.
Precisely because he destroys Smara and the rest, the God Hara is known as Smarahara.
Now, the consideration of Gaurī:
By her very nature she is the Left (Vāmā), beyond the reach of mind and speech;
as the left-limbed consort of Vāmadeva, Gaurī shines resplendent on his left side.
She is Bhavānī, the foremost among those who discourse on Brahman, a knower of Brahman herself,
who beholds everywhere with a sidelong glance that which is called Brahman, Śiva.
"She for whom the thought 'He is my beloved, my lord, my very self, and the master of my home' is fixed upon Śiva— she is the blessed Daughter of the Mountain."
He was gazed upon, he was embraced, he was fed, and he was honored;
that very Supreme Lord was meditated upon in the heart by Pārvatī.
Pārvatī worships Śiva with devotion through her fidelity as a wife;
therefore, her good fortune is celebrated in both the world and the Veda.
This yoga of the lords of yoga is experienced by Maheśvara;
endowed with that yoga, Bhavānī is a divine yoginī.
The Supreme Lord dances eternally before Pārvatī;
since such love exists within him, why would he not dance before her?
I bow to Bhavānī and Śaṅkara, who, though endowed with a single self-nature, abide as if they were of distinct natures, just like a knower of Brahman and his consort.
Pārvatī deserves praise for two reasons:
because of her love for Śaṅkara, and because of Śaṅkara’s love for her.
Pārvatī is especially worthy of worship even more than Śaṅkara;
she is the increaser of the bliss of him who is himself the manifest embodiment of bliss.
Pārvatī is indeed the very nature of the Supreme Brahman; there is no doubt about this, since Sadāśiva, the knower of Brahman, possesses abundant love for her.
In the groves are Mandāra trees; the moat-water is an ocean of nectar; at the gate are the eight supernatural powers; within the inner apartments is Pārvatī;

the trident is the best of weapons; the bull is his dear friend; the skull is in his hand; the necklace is poison; on his arms are serpents; and he has a fondness for the ash-smeared body as his ornament.
Triumphant over the light of a hundred moons and suns, radiant with the moon as her crest-jewel, bearing matted locks containing the Gaṅgā, three-eyed, and pure as the waters of the Gaṅgā;
accompanied on her left by the Daughter of the Mountain,
always adorned with prosperity, blissful in her own self, and possessing a blue throat— the form of the Destroyer of Cities flashes forth before me.
Thus, with its necessary adjuncts, meditation is the bath for Paśupati;
the latent impression of being a bound soul (paśu) is to be abandoned by the stream of the waters of the Ganges of knowledge.
Lord Śiva, the Lord of Creatures, should be bathed with pure and cool water.
"Salutation to Śiva"—thus is the worship performed.
"Śiva is the god, Śiva is the living soul; nothing exists other than Śiva.
In this manner, the anointing with sandalwood paste should be offered to Śiva with devotion. (NBs 50.84)

Now, regarding the *akṣatas* (unbroken grains): they are called *akṣatas* because they are unbroken; the Lord himself is indeed unbroken (*akṣata*). Therefore, Śiva is to be worshipped with *akṣatas* through devotion that is itself unbroken.
Now follows the consideration of the *arka* flower:
The *arka* is named Pāśupata, a deity dear to the Pāśupatas;
therefore, the flower of the Pāśupata *arka* is dear to Paśupati.
Whatever pungent-leaved tree was offered by a devotee to Giriśa,
that very thing became the sun— the illuminator and destroyer of darkness. (NBs 50.87)
When the flower of this pungent-leaved plant was offered by Śāmbhava, it was accepted by Śambhu; therefore, she became known as Śivamallikā.
Now, the determination regarding the thorn-apple (*dhattūra*):
By the grace of the Lord, the world appears in a different manner;
because it possesses qualities similar to his own, the thorn-apple is dear to Śiva.
Being herself free of the mind (unmanī) yet intoxicated, she intoxicates those who belong to Śambhu;
for this very reason, the flower produced from the Unmatta [plant] is dear to Śambhu.
This universal [nature] is not defiled by the deceit of this deceiver;
therefore, the flower of deceit is dear to the rogue of a gambler.
Desire and the other passions are great rogues by whom the three worlds have been robbed;
he who outwits them through skillful means is himself a rogue, beloved of Dhūrjaṭi.
Because this "rogue-leaf" (dhattūra), which bestows the merit of gold, was offered to Śaṅkara,
the dhattūra tree became known by the name "Gold" (kanaka).
Now follows the determination regarding Kaṇṭakārikā:
"If, through devotion, the mind's activity has been offered to Śaṅkara by a devotee, then even though it is by nature thorny, it becomes free from thorns. (NBs 50.94)

Now follows the consideration of the *bilva* tree: Indeed, because of his nature of devotion to Śiva, the great sage Śāṇḍilya [offered] that leaf which originates from the *śāṇḍilya* tree, for it is dear to Śambhu by that very name.
Mahādeva is the universal form, himself characterized as an actor;
therefore, he is pleased by the worship of actors' robes.
The fruit of one's birth, however, comes from offering the glorious bilva leaves to Śiva;
therefore, the bilva tree has been designated by the name "Śrīphala" (the Fruit of Fortune).
Incense, lamps, food offerings, fruit, betel, and ritual fees—
by simply saying "Salutation to Śiva," all of this constitutes his worship.
Among the sciences, the Veda is supreme; within the Veda, the Rudraikādaśinī is supreme;
therein, the five-syllabled mantra is the best. That should be recited for the gratification of Śiva.
The seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen— these three leaves,
when offered to Śiva whose nature is consciousness, constitute the first bilva leaf.
The second *bilva* leaf, accompanied by three inscriptions— “the agent,” “the action,” and “the instrument”— should be offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness.
The enjoyer, the act of eating, and the food— this third bilva leaf, consisting of these three parts, is to be offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness.
The fourth *bilva* leaf, consisting of the three leaves "Bhūr," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svaḥ," should be offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness. (NBs 50.103)
Having offered the three leaves— waking, dreaming,
and deep sleep— to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, one offers the fifth bilva leaf.
The sixty-fold bilva leaf, consisting of three layers known as the gross, the subtle, and the causal,
should be offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness.
Ignorance, transmigratory existence, and the individual soul—these three leaves are offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness; this is the seventh bilva leaf.
"Arising, persistence, and destruction—these three leaves are joined together;
indeed, this eighth bilva leaf is to be offered to Śiva, who is of the nature of consciousness. (NBs 50.107)
The ninth bilva leaf, endowed with three leaves representing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, should be offered to Śiva, who is the embodiment of consciousness.
Tamas, rajas, and likewise sattva—these constitute the three leaves;
the tenth bilva leaf is to be offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness.
"Thou-ness," "I-ness," and likewise "this-ness"—these three leaves are offered to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness; this is the bilva leaf known as Rudra.
These eleven bilva leaves are said to belong to Śambhu;
when Śambhu is worshipped with these, he immediately bestows liberation.
Now, the worship of the eight forms:
Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, Paśupati, Mahādeva, and Īśāna— this is the worship of the forms.
The eight forms of Prakṛti are the eightfold afflictions of the embodied soul;
clearly, through his eight manifestations, this Lord of Eight Forms (Aṣṭamūrti) removes them.
Now, the determination regarding circumambulation:
Mahādeva is infinite; even in hundreds of kalpas, one could not complete his circumambulation.
Therefore, half [of the path] is the circumambulation of Śiva.
Now, the consideration of backbiting (*gallavādya*):
Just as the true nature of the Lord cannot be described,
praise or backbiting— both are equal to Śambhu.

Now follows the investigation of prostration: Mahādeva is to be saluted with a prostration like a staff upon the ground through a state of overflowing love, because of the dissolution of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Now, the request for forgiveness:
"Even though having attained human birth, I have not worshipped Maheśvara;
a great offense has been committed—forgive me," one should say this repeatedly.
Now, the determination of the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*):
the dismissal of [the notions of] knowerhood, agenthood, enjoyerhood, and the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*)—this alone constitutes the dismissal in this worship of Śiva. (NBs 50.118)
The fourfold aims of human life come under one's command;
by whom can the greatness of this worship of Śiva be described? (NBs 50.119)
He who knows Śiva in reality knows the worship of Śiva;
but who knows Śiva in reality, and who knows the worship of Śiva?
The praise of the essence of awakening is that in which there is worship of the Guru at the beginning and the worship of Śiva at the end.
In the midst of this, the remembrance of Mukunda is the essence of awakening; that is the supreme.
"O dear one, a treatise such as this—one whose meaning is easy to understand and which is endowed with many distinctive features—has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. (NBs 51.2)
I neither praise nor blame; I speak according to how things truly are.
In each verse here, the definitive conclusion of the established doctrine is proclaimed.
Just as the entire essence of the universe is contained within every single atom,
so too is the entire essence of the established doctrine (siddhānta) set forth in every single verse.
It is the hoe that uproots ignorance, the forest fire for the dry grass of ignorance, the tiger for the deer of ignorance, and the lion for the elephant of ignorance. (NBs 51.5)
Ignorance is the venom of the living being, ignorance is the dagger at the throat;
ignorance is the water for the salt of existence, and ignorance is the ocean of dissolution.
He is the thunderbolt for the mountain of ignorance, the Śaṅkara who dispels the darkness of ignorance,
the Govinda who slew the Kaṃsa of ignorance, and the fierce Caṇḍikā against the savage ignorance.
This essence of awakening is the moon that cools the burning heat of ignorance, the sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance,
and likewise the one who awakens from the dream of ignorance.
The worship of the essence of awakening is my guru, for this essence of awakening is the bestower of knowledge upon me.
This Bodhasāra is my disciple, with whom I am speaking.
This Essence of Awareness is my master, who always protects me;
this Essence of Awareness is my servant, who performs service for me.
This Bodhasāra is my friend; he knows everything concerning me.
This Bodhasāra is my companion; when he is seen, I find happiness.
This essence of awakening is my home, where I dwell;
this essence of awakening is my garden, my monastery.
This essence of consciousness is my beloved, embracing whom I sleep;
this essence of consciousness is my mind, by which reflection is produced.
This intellect of mine, whose essence is awakening, by which the Supreme is understood;
this mind of mine, whose essence is awakening, by which I am conscious within that state.
The ego is the essence of consciousness; indeed, I am myself the essence of consciousness.
My body is the essence of consciousness, wherein my sense of "mine-ness" is most abundant.
This essence of awakening is my vital breath (prāṇa), in which my sense of "mine-ness" is most abundant;
this essence of awakening is my life-force (jīva), by which I always live.
The Essence of Consciousness is my Lord, for it bestows liberation upon me;
the Essence of Consciousness is the Supreme Brahman, and there is nothing higher than the Essence of Consciousness.
In order to establish the validity [of the Vedas],
having carefully distinguished each individual fragrant flower from those flowering mantra-trees that grow in the forest of the Upaniṣads;
This Bodha-liṅga was worshipped by the wise Nṛhari with the very flowers of his own compositions, in order to attain the state of the flavor of equanimity. // 1 //

Beneficial to wise people, following the traditional lineage, a treasury of supreme bliss, and the primary cause for liberation from delusion—let this *Bodhasāra*, composed by Narahari, which is water for the tree of awakening and an axe for the forest of evil intellect, be studied. // 2 //
For those initiated by gurus, everything indeed is an offering to the Lord;
however, this *Bodhasāra* is the very self of the Supreme Lord himself.
